Now the chair stands still. I sit on it every morning and eat my breakfast.

In the garden there are two swings and a long bench under a big tree.
There is a shop at the gate. It sells milk, eggs, bread and ice cream.
Old people sit on the bench in the afternoon. Children run around them and shout.

Across the road there is a hospital, a bank and a bus stop.
Everything I need is within ten minutes. That is why I like this place.
I can walk to school, to the shop and to the park.

Last week the strap of my school bag broke. He fixed it in five minutes and asked for two yuan.
I gave him five and said keep the change. He smiled and gave me an apple instead.

I would also make a small playground for dogs, and a place where old people can play chess.

The shop owner opens at seven. The nurse in the small clinic works until ten at night.
We do not always notice them, but the community stops working without them.

title: After We Help
paragraphs: Helping other people feels strange at first. You do not get anything back.
You give your time, and nobody pays you. You are tired and your hands are dirty.
But on the way home something is different. The street looks brighter. You walk faster.

title: Different Weather
paragraphs: The weather is not the same everywhere. In the north of China, winter is long and cold.
In the south, winter is short. Some years it does not snow at all.
In the west, the air is dry. In the east, it rains a lot in spring and summer.

title: A Rainy Day
paragraphs: It rained all day last Sunday. The sky was grey and the windows were wet.
We could not go out, so we stayed at home. My father made soup and my mother read a book.
I built a tall tower with my blocks. It fell down twice, and the third time it stood.
In the afternoon the rain stopped. The street was shiny, and the air smelled like stone.

title: April Weather
paragraphs: In April the weather cannot make up its mind. In the morning it is cold and windy.
By noon the sun is hot, and everyone takes off their jacket.
At four it turns dark and starts to rain. By six the rain has stopped and the sky is pink.
My mother says, in April, carry an umbrella and a coat. She is always right.

title: What to Wear
paragraphs: On a hot day, wear light clothes. Cotton is cool and it dries fast.
On a cold day, wear three layers. A shirt, a sweater, and a coat will keep you warm.
On a rainy day, take an umbrella and wear shoes that do not let water in.
On a windy day, wear something with a hood. It is better than a hat that flies away.

title: When the Typhoon Comes
paragraphs: In summer, typhoons come to the south. The radio tells us two days before.
We buy water, bread and candles. We move the plants from the balcony into the room.
Then we close every window and wait. The wind sounds like a train going past.
The next morning the street is full of leaves and broken branches. Neighbours clean together.

title: Weather and Feelings
paragraphs: Many people feel different in different weather. This is not strange.
On sunny days we go outside. We walk more and we meet more people, so we feel happier.
On grey days we stay in. We sleep more and talk less, and sometimes we feel heavy.

The second is need. Do you need it, or do you only want it?
The third is quality. A cheap pair of shoes that lasts one month is not cheap.

title: When Things Are on Sale

Before you buy, ask yourself two questions. Do I need it? Was it this price last week?
A good buyer is not the one who spends the least. It is the one who buys what he needs.

title: Why Do We Need Farms?
paragraphs: Everything we eat comes from a farm, a river, or the sea. There is no other place.
Rice needs warm rain and shallow water. Wheat needs a cold winter and a dry summer.
Vegetables come from small farms near cities. They are picked early and sold the same day.
When you eat lunch, you are eating the work of many people you will never meet.

title: One Day on the Farm
paragraphs: My uncle has a small farm. He gets up at five, before the sun.
First he feeds the chickens and lets them out. Then he walks around the fields and looks at the water.
At noon it is too hot to work. He rests for two hours, and so does everybody else.
In the afternoon he works again until it is dark. Then he sits outside and sleeps early.

title: Where Does Rice Come From?
paragraphs: Rice starts in a small box, not in a field. Farmers put seeds in wet soil and wait.
After about a month, the small plants are moved into the water field. This is called transplanting.
The plants grow tall. In autumn the field turns yellow, and the water is let out.
Then people cut the rice, dry it in the sun, and take it to a mill. Only then is it rice in a bag.

title: Machines on the Farm
paragraphs: Farms use many machines now. A tractor can do the work of twenty people in one day.
A machine can cut and thresh rice in a few hours. Before, this took a whole village a week.
But machines cost money, and they need petrol and repairs. Small farms often share one.
So the work is faster, but it is not free.

title: Farms and Cities

Now food travels hundreds of kilometres before it reaches a shop. It is cheap, but it is not fresh in the same way.

title: A Seed's Journey
paragraphs: A seed is a small thing, but it holds a whole plant inside.
It needs three things to start: water, warmth, and air. Without one of them, it waits.
Some seeds wait for years. They stay in the ground until the conditions are right.
Then the root comes out first, going down. The shoot comes second, going up. The plant knows which way is which.

title: How Do We Get Food?
paragraphs: Food does not appear in a shop. It comes from plants and animals on farms.
Some food we eat fresh: fruit, vegetables, eggs. Some we keep for a long time.
Milk becomes cheese and yoghurt. Wheat becomes flour and then bread. Pork is salted and dried.
So a farm does not only grow food. It also changes food into something that can travel.

title: Animals on the Farm

Ducks work in the wet fields. Pigs eat almost anything and grow fast.
A cow gives milk every day, but she must be milked at the same time each morning. A farm day has no holidays.

title: From Farm to Table

title: Farm Work in Four Seasons

Autumn is for harvesting. Everyone works, including children and old people.
Winter is for repair. Tools are fixed, the house is cleaned, and plans are made for spring.

title: The Friend from Another City

She spoke fast and used words we did not know. Some students laughed, but I do not think they meant to be unkind.
At lunch I asked her what Chengdu is like. She talked for twenty minutes without stopping.
Now she is the one who explains things to the rest of us. She knows more about the world than we do.

title: Choosing a Friend

Do not choose someone only because they are popular or funny. Popular changes. Funny gets old.
Choose someone who is happy when something good happens to you. That is rarer than it sounds.

title: Are Online Friends Real Friends?
paragraphs: Some of my classmates have friends they have never met. They talk every day through games and messages.
I think such a friend is a real friend, but a different kind. You can share ideas and jokes, and you can be kind.
But there is one thing you cannot do. You cannot see whether the other person is tired, or sad, or pretending.
So I would say this. An online friend is a door. A friend you can meet is a room.

title: When I Feel Nervous

Three things help me. First, breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in.
Second, move your fingers or your feet. Third, say the first sentence out loud in your head before you start.

title: What Anger Looks Like

The hands close into fists. The person stops listening and starts preparing an answer.
It is useful to notice this in yourself. If you can see it coming, you can step out of the room for one minute.
One minute is often enough. Anger needs to be fed, and if you stop feeding it, it goes down.

title: What Happiness Feels Like

There is the quiet kind: warm water on your hands in winter, a book you cannot put down, a friend who understands you without words.
The loud kind comes and goes quickly. The quiet kind lasts longer, and it is the one worth building a life around.

When you are worried, your shoulders go up and your stomach feels tight.
When you are tired of something, you look away and stop asking questions.
So if you want to know how someone really feels, do not only listen to their words. Look at their shoulders.

title: Learning to Say It

At first I said fine. After two months, I started saying other things.
It is strange, but saying I am angry makes the anger smaller. Saying nothing makes it bigger.

title: Work and Play

So an hour on the court is not an hour lost. It is an hour spent on something the body and the brain both need.

title: Why Sleep Matters
paragraphs: When you sleep, your body is not doing nothing. It is repairing and sorting.
Your brain moves what you learned today into longer storage. That is why a good night helps you remember.
Children need more sleep than adults, because their bodies are growing.
One late night will not hurt you. Five late nights in a row will, and you will not notice until the weekend.

title: Junk Food

You do not have to stop eating it. You only have to notice how often.
Once a week is a treat. Twice a day is a habit, and habits are hard to change later.

title: Washing Your Hands

Wash before you eat, after you use the toilet, and after you come home from outside.
Use soap and rub for at least twenty seconds. Most people rub for five.
Dry your hands properly. Wet hands pick up germs faster than dry ones.
This one small habit keeps more children in school than any medicine.

title: Choosing a Sport

title: Looking After Your Eyes

Second, follow the twenty-twenty rule. Every twenty minutes, look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds.
Reading in good light matters too, but daylight and distance matter more.

title: What We Eat
paragraphs: A good meal has three parts: something to give energy, something to build the body, and vegetables or fruit.
Rice, noodles and bread give energy. Meat, fish, eggs and beans build the body.
Vegetables and fruit give vitamins and something called fibre, which helps your stomach work.
Most meals in my home have all three. Not because we are careful, but because that is how my grandmother cooks.

title: Three Meals a Day
paragraphs: Breakfast is the meal most people skip, and it is the one that matters most for students.
After ten hours without food, your brain needs fuel. Children who eat breakfast concentrate better in the first two classes.
Lunch should be the biggest meal. Dinner should be earlier and smaller.

The others I know as sounds: a door, a washing machine, a chair moved at eleven at night.
This is normal in cities, and it is not a disaster. But it means that in a real emergency, nobody knows who is inside.
So say one sentence to the person next door. Not a friendship. Just enough to know a name.

title: A Notice on the Board
paragraphs: There is a notice board in our entrance. Most of it is adverts for locksmiths and English classes.
Last month a handwritten page appeared: piano lessons, free, for children over eight, on Sunday mornings.
It was gone in a week, replaced by a printed advert. But four children had already started, and they kept going.
A community changes when one person writes something by hand and signs it with a phone number.

title: My Favourite Season
paragraphs: People ask which season I like best, and I have stopped answering autumn, because it is not true.
What I like is the two weeks when one season is turning into another. The light changes, and the air smells different.
In late September the evenings come early and the food tastes better, and everybody is a little more awake.
A season on its own is only weather. The interesting part is the door between them.

title: Four Kinds of Rain
paragraphs: Spring rain is thin and goes on for hours. You do not need an umbrella, and then suddenly you do.
Summer rain arrives without warning, hits the ground hard, and is finished in twenty minutes.
Autumn rain is cold and quiet, and it makes people stay indoors without deciding to.
Winter rain is the worst kind, because it is almost snow and does not have the courage to be snow.

title: When the Season Changes
paragraphs: The change of season is not a date on a calendar. It is a set of small signals that arrive out of order.
The first one is usually light. You notice that the lamp is not needed at six, or that it is needed again.
Then come the clothes. Somebody wears a coat, and the next day half the class does too.
The calendar says one thing and the body says another, and the body is usually right.

title: Summer in the City
paragraphs: Summer in a city is hotter than summer in the country, and the reason is the surfaces.
Concrete and asphalt hold heat all day and give it back at night, so the city never really cools down.
This is why the parks matter more than they look. A row of trees can lower the street by three or four degrees.
In a hot city, shade is not decoration. It is the difference between walking and not walking.

title: Autumn Came Early
paragraphs: This year the leaves turned in the last week of September, which is three weeks earlier than usual.
My grandmother noticed before anyone. She said the birds had gone, and she was right.
The market changed too. The chestnuts arrived early, and the man who sells them said the whole year was early.
Farmers do not read the calendar to decide when to harvest. They read the field, and this year the field was in a hurry.

title: Winter Clothes
paragraphs: Winter clothes are not really about warmth. Three thin layers are warmer than one thick one, and easier to carry.
The layer next to your skin should take sweat away. The middle one holds air. The outer one stops the wind.
Most people wear too much indoors and too little outdoors, which is why so many people are ill in December.
So dress for the room you are going into, not for the one you are leaving.

title: The First Warm Day
paragraphs: There is one day in March when the wind changes and everybody knows it at the same time.
Coats come off on the way home. People sit outside shops. Somebody opens a window that has been shut since November.
The temperature is usually only fifteen degrees. It is not warm. It only feels warm, because of what came before.
That is the strange thing about weather. You do not feel it on its own. You feel it against yesterday.

title: Seasons and Memory
paragraphs: Some memories are tied to a season, and you cannot separate them.
I cannot think of winter without thinking of my grandmother's soup. I cannot think of summer without the sound of a fan.
This is strange, because the soup and the fan were not important things.
But memory does not keep the important things. It keeps what was there, again and again, for years.

title: My Hometown
paragraphs: My hometown is a small city with one river, two bridges, and a factory that closed in 2011.
It is not beautiful and it is not famous. People who visit for a day usually say there is nothing to do.
What they miss is that the town is a set of habits. Where you buy breakfast, which road you avoid at six, who fixes shoes.
A hometown is not a place you can see. It is a place you know your way around without thinking.

title: What Changed and What Did Not
paragraphs: I went back after four years. The road was wider, the old bus station was a car park, and there was a new school.
The shop at the corner was still there, with the same man behind the counter, ten years older.
He did not remember me until I said my mother's name, and then he asked about her in detail.
Places change quickly and people change slowly. When you go back, the buildings are the strangers.

title: The River Behind the Town
paragraphs: When I was small the river behind the town was where everyone went in summer.
There was a low bridge, and boys jumped off it, and mothers stood on the bank pretending not to watch.
Then the factory upstream grew, the water changed colour, and the swimming stopped. Nobody made an announcement.
It closed in 2011. The water is clean again now, but the children who swam there have grown up and moved away.

title: The Market on Sunday
paragraphs: The Sunday market is the only place in my hometown where you can hear four dialects in one minute.
Vegetables on the left, fish at the back, and in the middle a man who has sold the same three kinds of noodles for years.
Prices are not written anywhere. They depend on who you are, which is unfair and also the point.
By eleven it is finished. The square becomes a square again, and there is nothing but wet ground and cardboard.

title: Why People Leave
paragraphs: Everyone in my class has left the town. The reasons sound similar when you say them out loud.
Work, mostly. Then school for the children. Then the fact that once you leave, coming back is harder each year.
People say the young have no feeling for their hometown. That is not true. They have a very strong feeling and no way to use it.
So they come back for four days at New Year, and the town fills up, and then it empties again.

title: Coming Back
paragraphs: My uncle came back at forty-two, after eighteen years in the city, and opened a small restaurant.
Everyone said it was a mistake. The town has too few customers and too many restaurants.
He said he knew. He said he was tired of eating alone in a city where he knew nobody on his floor.
Three years later the restaurant is still open, just. He is not rich. He is not alone either.

title: The Food of My Hometown
paragraphs: Every hometown has one dish that people argue about, and the argument is about a small thing.
In my town it is a soup. Half the families put in vinegar first, half put it in at the end, and both say the other is wrong.
The recipe is not written down. It is learned standing next to somebody in a kitchen.
This is why the food tastes different when you make it elsewhere, even with the same things. Nobody taught you with their hands.

title: A Map of My Hometown
paragraphs: If I drew a map of my hometown, it would not look like the ones in books.
It would have the long way to school, which is the safe way, and the short way, which is through a hole in a wall.
It would mark the shop where you can buy one thing, and the bench where old men play cards every afternoon.
Maps show roads. What people remember is where something happened, and that is a different drawing.

title: Travelling Around the Province
paragraphs: People save for years to travel abroad and never visit the county three hours away.
In that county there is a mountain, a temple from the Ming period, and a kind of noodle you cannot get anywhere else.
The advantage of travelling near is time. You lose no day to the airport, and you can go back if you like it.
The disadvantage is that you do not feel brave. But feeling brave is not the same as seeing something new.

title: By Train or by Bus
paragraphs: For a journey of three hours, the train and the bus cost about the same, and the choice depends on one thing.
The bus leaves from the middle of the town and arrives in the middle of the next one. The train station is always outside.
So by the time you have paid for two taxi rides, the bus is cheaper, even though its ticket looks more expensive.
Always count the whole journey, not the part with the ticket.

title: The Long Way Round
paragraphs: The map showed a straight road along the coast and a longer one that went up into the hills.
We took the hills because a man at the petrol station said the coast road was closed. He was wrong.
The coast road was open. We spent two extra hours on a road with no view and a lot of goats.
It turned out to be the best part of the trip. There was a village at the top with a shop and a dog and nothing else.

title: What to Pack
paragraphs: Most people pack for the weather they hope for, and then buy the things they actually need at the other end.
For three days away you need three of everything, one warm layer, and one pair of shoes you can walk in.
The heaviest thing in most bags is the thing people take in case. Take one of those, not five.
And leave a little space. A bag that comes back full is a bag that was packed correctly.

title: Travelling With a Group
paragraphs: A tour group sees six places in three days and remembers two of them.
The bus is comfortable, the price is fixed, and nobody has to decide anything. That is the whole offer.
The cost is attention. When forty people arrive at a temple at the same time, nobody can look at anything quietly.
Groups are good for the first visit to a place. Go back alone if you want to know it.

title: The Place Nobody Told Me About
paragraphs: In a town I visited last year, the famous building was closed for repairs, so I walked in the wrong direction.
Two streets away there was a workshop making paper umbrellas. Three people worked there and one of them spoke to me.
He showed me how the bamboo ribs are bent, and said his father had done the same thing in the same room.
I stayed an hour. It was not on any list, and it is the only thing I remember from that town.

title: A Day in a Strange City
paragraphs: I had one day in a city I had never seen, and no plan except a train at eight in the evening.
I bought a ticket for the bus, got off where the buildings looked old, and walked until I was hungry.
I ate where the menu had no pictures and pointed at what the next table was having. It was very good.
By four I was tired and had seen nothing famous. It was the best day of the whole trip.

title: Getting Lost on Purpose
paragraphs: Getting lost is only frightening when you have an appointment. Without one, it is the cheapest way to see a city.
The rule is to keep the sun on the same side, or to remember one tall building, and never to hurry.
Walk down the street that looks less interesting. Turn where there is a shop with no English on the sign.
You will not find anything. That is fine. You are not looking for a place. You are learning the shape of one.

title: Making a Travel Plan
paragraphs: A travel plan has four parts, and most people only write the first one.
Where you go, when you go, how you get there, and what you do if it rains. The fourth part is the useful one.
Write the plan on one page. If it needs two pages, you have written a wish, not a plan.
And leave one afternoon empty. Something always takes longer than you think, and an empty afternoon saves the day.

title: The Plan That Changed
paragraphs: Our plan had six places in two days. We did the first one in the morning and it took until two.
So we crossed out four places and sat in a park instead, and my father was annoyed for about an hour.
In the evening we found a night market by accident, which was not on the plan at all.
Now I write plans with three things a day, not six. The two spare things are the ones that happen.

title: How Much Will It Cost?
paragraphs: When people guess the cost of a trip, they add up the tickets and forget everything else.
There is the ticket, the bed, the food, the local transport, and the small things you buy without deciding to.
The small things are usually ten to twenty percent. Add them at the start, not at the end, when it is too late.
Then add a quarter more. Not because things will go wrong, but because they always cost a little more than the guess.

title: Booking a Room
paragraphs: A photograph of a room tells you three things: the colour of the wall, the size of the bed, and nothing else.
Read the lowest recent review instead. It will tell you about the noise, the water pressure, and the walk to the bus.
Book somewhere near the station for the first night, even if it costs more.
And write down the address in the local language. You will need it in a taxi, and you will not be able to say it.

title: One Day, Three Places
paragraphs: Three places in one day is the right number, and two of them should be close together.
Morning is for the place that will be crowded. Afternoon is for the one that needs attention. Evening is for walking.
Do not plan a museum after four o clock. The legs are tired and the eyes stop taking things in.
And plan the meal. A day with no planned meal becomes an hour of argument in the street at seven.

title: Who Carries the Plan
paragraphs: Amy: I have the plan on my phone. Ben: And if your phone dies? Amy: You have it on paper.
Ben: I do not have it on paper. Amy: That is why I printed two copies. One is in your bag.
Ben: What is the first thing tomorrow? Amy: The temple at eight, before the groups arrive.
Ben: Eight? Amy: Eight. You can sleep on the train in the afternoon, which is also on the plan.

title: The Day We Stayed In
paragraphs: On the third day it rained so hard that the streets were rivers and the buses stopped.
Our plan had a mountain on it. We crossed it out and stayed in the room, playing cards and eating biscuits.
By the afternoon we were bored, and boredom turned out to be useful. We talked for three hours without a screen.
The mountain is still there. My sister and I still talk about the card game.

title: After the Trip
paragraphs: The part of a trip nobody plans is the part after it: the photographs, the receipts, and the bag you do not unpack.
Do one thing on the first evening back. Empty the bag, put the washing in, and write five lines about the trip.
The five lines are worth more than two hundred photographs you will never look at.
A trip ends twice. Once when you come home, and once when you stop talking about it. The five lines delay the second one.

title: A Week of Small Trips
paragraphs: Last spring my family did something cheap. Instead of one long trip, we did four short ones.
Each was under two hours away: a lake, an old village, a hill with a temple, and a market town.
We left after breakfast and were home for dinner. Nobody was tired, and nobody had to pack.
By the end of the month we had seen more than we would have seen in one week away, and spent less.

title: The Best Plan I Ever Made
paragraphs: The best plan I ever made was for four people and one day, and it fitted on a card.
It had three places, two meals, one bus, and a rain option. It also had the phone numbers of two people who lived there.
What made it good was not the detail. It was that everyone had read it before we left, so nobody had to ask.
A plan is not a schedule. It is a way of stopping four people from having the same argument in a street.

title: Better Than the Photos
paragraphs: The photos of the lake were everywhere last summer. Blue water, white boats, and not one person in the picture.
When we got there, the car park was full and the boats were queued three deep. My father laughed and said, of course.
We walked twenty minutes past the boats and found a small stone beach. Nobody was there. The water was the same blue.
Now I look at travel photos differently. I look at the edges of the picture, where the crowd has been cut out.

title: The First Time I Saw the Sea
paragraphs: I was nine when I first saw the sea. We had driven five hours and I had asked, how much longer, at least twenty times.
Then the road turned and there it was, flat and grey and enormous, moving in a way a lake never moves.
We stayed two hours. I did not swim much. Mostly I stood at the edge and let the water come to my feet and go back.
On the way home I fell asleep at once. My father says I talked about waves in my sleep for half the journey.

title: Why Old Towns Look Alike
paragraphs: Visit three old towns in three provinces and you will start to feel you have been to the same one.
Stone streets, wooden shop fronts, red lanterns, and a shop selling the same ginger sweets in every town.
But part of it is new. In the last twenty years many of them were repaired to look old rather than kept old.
So when you go, look for the parts nobody photographed: a wall with different bricks, or a door with two kinds of paint.

title: Three Hours on a Mountain
paragraphs: The path up was not difficult. It was just long, and the top never seemed any closer.
At the first rest point an old man was selling water and boiled eggs from a basket. He said, forty minutes more, and smiled.
We reached the top in an hour and a half. There was a stone with a name on it, three other families, and a very good wind.
Coming down took fifty minutes and hurt more than going up. Nobody tells you that part in advance.

title: The Museum Nobody Visits
paragraphs: Every city has a famous museum with a queue, and a quiet one with a guard asleep at the door.
The quiet one is usually about something narrow: fans, or bridges, or the history of the local newspaper.
Because it is narrow, it can go deep. One room of folding fans can teach you more about a place than ten rooms of pots.
So put one small museum on your list. It will not be the photo you show people, but it will be the hour you remember.

title: Travelling With My Grandmother
paragraphs: My grandmother is seventy-four and had not left the province for thirty years. Last spring she came with us to Xiamen.
She was not interested in the sea. She was interested in the market, and in how the fish were kept cold.
On the last night she told me about the first train she ever took, in 1968, and how many hours it took.
That hour on the wall was the best part of the trip for me. We had gone a thousand kilometres to sit still.

title: What I Bring Back
paragraphs: My aunt brings back magnets. Her fridge is a map of twenty years of trips, and every magnet is a small flag.
I bring back tickets. Bus tickets, museum tickets, a receipt from a noodle shop with the price written by hand.
Both of us are doing the same thing: keeping proof that we were somewhere. The difference is only the shape of the proof.
Souvenirs are not for other people. They are notes you leave for the person you will be in ten years.

title: The Place I Would Not Go Again
paragraphs: There is a beach I will not go back to, although the water is clean and the sand is white.
The reason is small. It takes two buses and a motorbike, four hours in total, and the last bus leaves at five.
So you spend the whole day watching the clock. The beach is beautiful and you cannot enjoy it, because you are doing arithmetic.
A place an hour away is worth more than a place four hours away, even if the second one is twice as beautiful.

title: Writing an Invitation
paragraphs: Dear Ben, I am going to have a small party at my flat on Saturday, the eighteenth, from three to six.
There will be food, but not a meal, so do not come hungry. My mother is making dumplings and my father is in charge of music.
You do not need to bring anything. If you want to, bring the card game you showed me last month.
If you cannot come, that is completely fine. Just tell me, so I do not keep a chair empty. Yours, Amy.

title: The Party That Started Late
paragraphs: The invitation said six o clock. By six fifteen nobody had arrived, and I was moving chairs around for no reason.
At six fifty the first three people arrived together, because they had all taken the same wrong bus.
By seven the room was full and nobody remembered the time. The food was cold and nobody cared.
I learned two things. Always give people a map, and never start eating the peanuts before your guests.

title: Saying Yes and Saying No
paragraphs: When a friend invites you, there are three answers, not two: yes, no, and yes but not that day.
Most people only use two. They say yes to everything and then cancel at the last minute, which is worse than saying no.
So when you cannot come, say it early, say why in one sentence, and suggest another time if you mean it.
Being invited again next month matters more than attending this week.

title: A Family Dinner
paragraphs: On Sunday eleven of us sat around one table, which meant two tables pushed together and one chair in the doorway.
My uncle arrived last, as always, carrying a bag of oranges nobody had asked for.
There were four dishes I could name and three I could not. The ones I could not were the ones that disappeared first.
At nine the table was cleared and half of us were still sitting there, talking about nothing, because leaving takes effort.

title: Meeting an Old Friend
paragraphs: I had not seen Chen for six years. We met at a coffee shop near the school we used to go to.
The first ten minutes were strange. We looked at each other and asked about work, and it was too polite.
We talked for three hours about people we had not thought about in years. Two of them we could not name.
I do not think we will meet again soon. But it was good to know that six years does not change the important part.

title: The Guest Who Came Early
paragraphs: The invitation said seven. At half past five the doorbell rang and there was my cousin, two hours early, holding a cake.
She put the cake down and started washing the dishes. We cleaned for forty minutes without talking much.
By the time the others arrived, we had finished, and she was sitting down like a guest, with a cup of tea.
Now when I am early, I stand at the corner for ten minutes. It is the kindest thing an early person can do.

title: After Everyone Leaves
paragraphs: The last guest left at ten past eleven. The door closed and the flat was suddenly very quiet.
There were forty cups, three plates with food still on them, and a chair that had been broken and put back together.
My mother and I cleaned for half an hour and then sat down on the floor, because the chairs were all wet.
The flat smelled of food for two days. That, more than the photos, is what I remember of the party.

title: How Do You Feel Today
paragraphs: Adults ask children how they feel, but they usually accept one word. Fine. Okay. Tired.
A single word hides a lot. Someone can be fine because nothing is wrong, or fine because they do not want to explain.
So if you want a real answer, ask a smaller question. What was the best part of today? When did you feel worst?
This works both ways. If someone asks how you are, you may give them two sentences instead of one word.

title: Sleep Is Not a Luxury
paragraphs: Many students treat sleep as the thing you give up when there is too much to do. That is the wrong way round.
You should keep the same bedtime on school nights and at weekends. Sleeping until noon on Sunday only moves the problem.
And you should not use a phone in bed. The screen keeps your brain awake for an hour after you put it down.
Eight hours is not a rule for weak people. It is what the body uses to turn work into memory.

title: Ten Thousand Steps
paragraphs: The number ten thousand did not come from medicine. It came from a Japanese step counter sold in the nineteen sixties.
That does not mean walking is useless. It means the exact number is a marketing figure, not a health law.
What matters is that you move every day, and that you move enough to be slightly out of breath once in a while.
So do not count to ten thousand. Notice whether you sat down all day, and if you did, go out before dinner.

title: Why Breakfast Matters
paragraphs: Breakfast is not magic. It does not make you thinner or smarter. But skipping it changes how the morning goes.
After ten hours without food, your body has little energy ready. You can still work, but it costs more effort.
You do not need a big breakfast. Bread, an egg, and a glass of milk take four minutes and are enough.
If you have no time, the answer is to get up ten minutes earlier, not to skip the meal.

title: Sitting All Day
paragraphs: Sitting is not dangerous because of one hour. It is dangerous because of nine hours in a row.
The body was not designed to stay in one shape. Blood moves less, the back takes the weight, and the eyes stop looking far away.
You should stand up every forty minutes, even for two minutes. Walk to the window, look far off, sit down again.
This is easier at school than at home, because school at least makes you walk between rooms.

title: When You Are Ill
paragraphs: Mum: You are warm. Stay home today.
Tom: But we have the maths test. Mum: The test will happen again. Today will not.
Tom: What should I do? Mum: Drink water, sleep, and do not look at your phone for six hours.
Tom: Six hours? Mum: You should rest your eyes too. They are part of your body, in case you had forgotten.
Tom: And the homework? Mum: I will write to your teacher. That is my job today, not yours.

title: Water
paragraphs: You should drink water before you are thirsty. Thirst arrives late, like a message that was sent an hour ago.
Sweet drinks do not count. They give you water and sugar together, and the sugar is the part your body did not ask for.
Keep a bottle on the desk and fill it twice a day. Do not wait for a system. Just keep it in sight.
Nothing about this is difficult. It is only easy to forget, which is why the bottle has to be visible.

title: The Habit I Broke
paragraphs: For two years I drank a sweet drink every afternoon. Not because I was thirsty, but because four o clock felt like a wall.
I did not decide to stop. I decided to change one thing: I put a bottle of water where the can used to sit.
What surprised me was not the change in my body. It was how much of the habit was about the walk to the shop.
So if you want to break something, do not fight it. Move the thing you reach for, and let your hand learn a new path.

title: My First Pocket Money
paragraphs: I was eight when I got pocket money for the first time. Ten yuan a week, on Sunday evening, in cash.
By Wednesday I had nothing, and there were four days to go. That week taught me more than any lesson about saving.
The next month I did something simple. I put two yuan in a tin on Sunday and spent the rest without thinking.
By the summer the tin had enough for a book I wanted. It was the first thing I owned that I had waited for.

title: A Spending Plan
paragraphs: A spending plan is not a list of things you cannot buy. It is a decision made in advance so you do not decide in a shop.
Divide your money into three parts: what you must spend, what you are saving for, and what you can waste.
The third part matters. A plan with no waste in it will break in the second week and you will blame the plan.
Review it once a month. Two minutes is enough, and it stops small leaks from becoming a hole.

title: Why Cheap Things Cost More
paragraphs: A pair of shoes for forty yuan that lasts three months costs more than a pair for two hundred that lasts two years.
This is easy to see afterwards and hard to see in the shop, because in the shop you only see the price today.
The rule is not to buy the most expensive thing. It is to think about how many times you will use it.
Divide the price by the number of uses and the answer is usually clear. A cheap thing used twice is the worst buy.

title: The Thing I Saved For
paragraphs: I saved for seven months for a pair of football boots. They cost four hundred and twenty yuan.
I did not do anything clever. I stopped buying drinks at the shop and put the money in a box instead.
In the fourth month I nearly spent it on a game. I did not, but I thought about it for three days.
They were not the best boots I ever had, and I wore them for two seasons. But I remember the counting, not the boots.

title: Lending Money to a Friend
paragraphs: Lending money to a friend is not a money problem. It is a friendship problem that happens to involve money.
Before you lend, decide one thing: can you afford to lose this amount and the friend? If not, lend less.
Say the date out loud. Not soon, not next week, but the fifteenth. A vague date is how friendships get damaged.
And if you are the one borrowing, pay back early. It costs nothing and it buys you something money cannot.

title: What Ads Do
paragraphs: An advertisement is not trying to tell you about a product. It is trying to give you a feeling and then attach the product to it.
That is why so many ads show friends laughing, or a family at a table, and almost never show the thing being used.
One question defeats most of them. What problem does this actually solve? If there is no answer, you are being sold a feeling.
You can still buy it. Just know which part you are paying for.

title: Two Weeks Without Snacks
paragraphs: For two weeks I did not buy anything between meals. Not as a diet, but to see how much I was spending.
The first three days were easy. On the fourth day I stood in front of the shop for a full minute and then walked away.
I wrote down every time I wanted something. In fourteen days there were nineteen entries, and eleven were after eight.
I still buy snacks. But now I know that most of my money was not going on hunger. It was going on being tired.

title: Paying for Your Own Phone
paragraphs: The moment you pay for your own phone, the phone stops being a gift and becomes a monthly decision.
Most students pay for the phone once, through their parents, and never see the second cost, which comes every month.
Sit down and add it up: the phone, the data, the case, the repairs, and the apps. The number is usually surprising.
Paying a repeating cost teaches more than paying a large one, because the lesson comes back every month.

title: Why We Look Up
paragraphs: Every culture has looked up and made up a story. The stars were animals, gods, or the eyes of people who had died.
We now know what most of them are: balls of gas, rocks, and light that left home before we were born.
Knowing this did not end the wonder. It changed it. The sky became larger and stranger than the stories.
So looking up is not childish. It is the oldest habit humans have, and we still do it with better instruments.

title: A Day on the Space Station
paragraphs: Astronauts do not float because there is no gravity. They float because they are falling around the Earth at great speed.
They exercise for two hours a day. Without it, bones and muscles weaken within a few weeks.
Eating is difficult. Water forms balls, crumbs float into machines, and salt and pepper are kept as liquids in a bottle.
They sleep in bags fixed to the wall. Everything is fixed to something, including the people.

title: The Moon Is Moving Away
paragraphs: The Moon is moving away from the Earth at about four centimetres a year. That is the speed your nails grow.
It is caused by the tides. The Moon pulls the oceans, the Earth spins, and slowly some of that energy is passed to the Moon.
Four centimetres sounds small, and it is. But it has been happening for four billion years.
One day, very far from now, a total solar eclipse will no longer be possible. The Moon will be too small in the sky.

title: What a Telescope Does
paragraphs: A telescope does not make things bigger. It makes them brighter and clearer, which is usually more useful.
That is why a telescope shows faint things. A distant galaxy is too dim for the eye, but it is not too small.
In a city the main problem is not the telescope but the light. You can see the Moon and a few planets, and not much else.
Take the same telescope twenty kilometres out of the city and the sky fills up. The instrument did not change. The darkness did.

title: Rockets Are Mostly Fuel
paragraphs: Look at a rocket on the launch pad and you are mostly looking at a fuel tank with a small payload on top.
Getting to orbit is not about going up. It is about going sideways fast enough, about eight kilometres a second.
That takes an enormous amount of energy, and most of it is spent lifting the fuel you have not burned yet.
It is also why reusing a rocket matters. A rocket thrown away after one flight is like a plane thrown away after one trip.

title: Is There Anybody Else?
paragraphs: The honest answer is that we do not know. The dishonest answer is that we do, and it is only a matter of time.
We know the conditions for life as we understand it: liquid water, energy, and enough time. Billions of planets may have these.
But might is not the same as does. So far we have found no signal, no microbe, nothing.
That one example is us. Until we find a second, every answer is a story with a number attached.

title: Two Skies
paragraphs: I grew up in the city and thought the night sky had about thirty stars. I could name three of them.
There were too many stars. The sky was crowded, and the Milky Way was a band of light, not a word in a book.
I stood there for twenty minutes and felt something I had never felt about the sky before, which was smallness.
Now in the city I notice the orange glow above the buildings. It is the reason thirty was all I ever saw.

title: Is Space Worth the Money?
paragraphs: People often ask why we spend billions on space when there are problems on Earth. It is a fair question.
The second is that the money is not sent into space. It pays engineers, factories and universities in the same country.
The third is the technology. Weather satellites, navigation, and the materials in your phone all came from this work.
None of this answers the moral question. But it turns a simple choice into a real argument about priorities.

title: Where the Electricity Comes From
paragraphs: When you press a switch, the electricity is not made at that moment. It was made a second earlier, somewhere else.
Most of it comes from burning coal or gas, which turns water into steam, which turns a turbine.
The grid has almost no storage. Supply must match demand every second, which is why engineers watch it like a heartbeat.
So the question is not whether you use electricity. It is what was burned, or not burned, to make it.

title: The Cost of a Plastic Bottle
paragraphs: A plastic bottle costs about one yuan. The oil inside it took millions of years to form and a few minutes to make.
You will use it for maybe fifteen minutes. In the sea it will stay for four hundred years, breaking into smaller pieces.
Recycling helps, but only a small share of bottles become new bottles. Most turn into lower-grade plastic.
The cheapest solution is still the oldest one. Carry a bottle and fill it.

title: Turn It Off
paragraphs: Standing by does not mean off. A television on standby still uses power, all night, every night.
You should turn off the screen and the socket, not just the remote. One device is small. Five for ten hours is not.
None of this will save the planet on its own. But habits spread, and a person who turns things off notices other waste.
Start with one socket you can reach without thinking. That is enough for the first month.

title: Wind and Sun
paragraphs: Wind and solar power are cheap now, but they are not always there. The wind stops and the Sun goes down.
That is the real problem with them. A coal plant can run all night. A solar farm cannot.
In a country as large as China, the wind is always blowing somewhere. Long distance lines move the power where it is needed.
The change is not about one perfect machine. It is about a system that can be steady without burning anything.

title: What a Tree Is Worth
paragraphs: A tree is worth more standing than cut. That sentence is easy to say and hard to put on a receipt.
Cut, it becomes furniture or paper, and the money appears at once, which is why the wrong choice keeps being made.
Cities are learning this. Some now count the shade and the water a tree holds, and pay to keep it.
So when a road is widened and the trees go, the cost is not only the trees. It is everything they were quietly doing.

title: Sorting the Rubbish
paragraphs: Sorting rubbish only works if the next step works. If the truck collects everything together, people stop sorting in a month.
Kitchen waste is the biggest share in most cities, and the easiest to turn into something useful.
The hardest part is not knowledge. Everyone knows what a bottle is. The hard part is doing it at nine at night.
So put the bins where you stand, not where they look neat. Design changes behaviour more than posters do.

title: The City That Banned Bags
paragraphs: In 2002 a city in Ireland put a small tax on plastic shopping bags. Nobody expected it to work.
Within a year the number of bags handed out fell by more than ninety percent. People did not stop shopping. They brought bags.
The interesting part is what happened next. The money from the tax paid for environmental projects people could see.
A rule works better when the money and the reason both go somewhere you can see.

title: Small Changes, Many People
paragraphs: One person turning off a light changes almost nothing. Ten million people doing it changes what a power station burns.
This is why individual habits matter, but not in the way people usually claim.
People who sort their rubbish are more likely to support a recycling scheme. People who walk to school ask for a safe crossing.
So do the small thing, but do not stop there. The small thing is a beginning, not an answer.

title: Learning in a Museum
paragraphs: A museum is a strange kind of classroom: no desks, no bell, and nobody tells you what to remember.
That is also its advantage. You choose what to look at, and you stay as long as you like.
The mistake is trying to see everything. A large museum in one afternoon is a walk, not a lesson.
Choose one room. Look at four objects. For each, ask three questions: what is it, who used it, and how did it get here.
Then leave. One room remembered is worth more than twelve rooms photographed.

title: The Object That Told a Story
paragraphs: In a small museum last year I saw a school exercise book from 1937. It belonged to a girl of eleven.
The writing was careful. In the margin there was a drawing of a bird, done when the lesson was boring.
Next to it was her report card, and a photograph of a class of forty children, all looking in different directions.
That is what an object can do that a paragraph cannot. It makes a stranger suddenly ordinary, and therefore real.

title: The Table by the Window
paragraphs: Every Sunday my grandmother sets the table by the window, even when only four of us are coming.
She puts out eight bowls. My mother says, we are only four. My grandmother says, the bowls are for the ones who might come.
Sometimes an uncle does come, or a cousin from the next town, and then she is right and nobody says anything about the bowls.
I used to think those extra bowls were a waste of washing. Now I think they are the reason people keep coming back.

title: Happy Together, Not All Day
paragraphs: Living together is not the same as being together all day, and most families find this out slowly.
A family that shares one room has no place to be alone. Small things become big things by evening.
So the best homes are not the biggest ones. They are the ones with a door that closes and a table that is shared.
Time apart is not a sign of a cold family. It is what makes the shared hours worth waiting for.

title: A Long Way for One Meal
paragraphs: My uncle works in a city nine hundred kilometres away. Every winter he takes a night train home for one dinner.
The train arrives at five in the morning. He sleeps three hours, then helps my aunt cut vegetables all afternoon.
At the table he says very little. He just keeps looking at everyone, the way you look at a place you have missed.
On the third day he takes the night train back. Nobody asks why he comes. Everybody already knows why.

title: The Loudest Room in the House

Sometimes she puts a piece of fish in his bowl, and he says thank you in three words of her language he learned last year.

title: The Photo Everyone Hates

title: Why We Sing Together
paragraphs: People have sung together for thousands of years, and not only for entertainment.
When a group sings, everyone breathes at the same time. Slow songs slow the heart a little, and loud songs speed it up.
Singing also makes a group feel like one group. Soldiers, workers and students have all used it for this reason.
You do not need a good voice to join in. You need to be in the room, close enough to hear the people beside you.

title: The Guest Who Stayed a Week

By the fourth day he was making breakfast and my mother was complaining about him like family.
He still calls every Spring Festival. My mother says, that man ate our rice for a week, and then she laughs.

title: Small Parties
paragraphs: A party of sixty people is mostly work. A party of six is mostly talk.
With six people there is one conversation. Everyone hears everything, so nobody has to tell a story twice.
With sixty there are ten conversations, and you spend the evening moving between them without finishing any.
So when you want to be happy together, invite fewer people. The food can be simple and the chairs do not matter.

title: Saying Thank You Properly
paragraphs: Thank you is a small phrase, and most people say it too fast, in a voice that means nothing.
A proper thank you names the thing: thank you for waiting for me in the rain for twenty minutes.
It also says what changed: because of that, I did not miss the last bus home.
And it asks for nothing back. A thank you with a request inside it is not really a thank you.

title: Why the Mooncake Is Round
paragraphs: A mooncake is round like the moon, and round also means whole, complete, all the family in one place.
Inside there is often a salted egg yolk. It stands for the full moon in the middle of the night sky.
The cake is heavy and sweet, and one small piece is enough. That is the point: it is food for sharing, not for eating alone.
So when a box arrives at your door, count the cakes before you count the days.

title: The Silk Road in a Market

The man at the corner sells walnuts and grapes. Another sells cucumbers, and another sells sesame cakes.
All of these came from far away, a thousand years ago, on the backs of camels.
So the next time you eat a cucumber, remember that it travelled further than most of us ever will.

Inside, the walls are covered with paintings a thousand years old. The guide holds up a small light and the colours come out.
Blue, green, red, and a gold that is still gold. Some of the paint was made from stone ground into powder.
We were allowed fifteen minutes in each cave. I spent mine looking at one dancer's hand.

The first hundred metres were a disaster. Half the boat pulled early and the other half pulled late, and we went sideways.
By the end of the afternoon we had made one good stroke together. The old men on the bank clapped as if we had won.

Red is for good fortune, and the paper is new because the old year has gone.
Nobody in my family can write them well, so we walk to the old man at the end of the lane. He writes for free.

The paper keeps the wind out, so the flame burns slowly. The frame keeps the paper away from the flame.
That is the whole invention, and it is a thousand years old. Later versions used oil, and now most use a bulb.
But the shape has not changed, because the shape is what people remember when they think of a festival.

The second month we learned to jump on the wooden benches. Two people fell, and one broke a wrist.
The third month we learned to blink the eyes and move the ears. That is when the lion stopped looking like a costume.

title: Keeping a Tradition Alive
paragraphs: A tradition dies in two ways. The first is that nobody remembers it. The second is that everybody performs it for tourists.

The traditions that survive are the ones people still use at home: a dish for a birthday, a song for a boat, a paper on a door.
So if you want to keep something, do not put it in a museum. Cook it, sing it, and teach it to somebody small.

title: The Shop That Closed
paragraphs: The shop at the corner of our lane sold everything: salt, batteries, string, and ice cream for one yuan.
Old Chen sat behind the counter from six in the morning until ten at night, for thirty years.
Then the supermarket opened eight hundred metres away, and people stopped walking to the corner.

paragraphs: A letter takes three days and has to be thought about. A message takes one second and often is not thought about at all.
This is not only a change of speed. It is a change in what we expect from each other.
When a letter arrived, the whole family read it and someone wrote back the same evening.
Now a message can arrive during dinner, and the polite thing is to answer it before the soup gets cold.

title: My Grandmother's Kitchen
paragraphs: My grandmother cooked on a brick stove that burned wood. The smoke went up through a pipe in the roof.
The fire had to be watched. Rice needs a strong fire first, then a low one, and the last ten minutes with no wood at all.
She could tell the temperature by putting her hand above the pot and counting seconds.
Her new kitchen has a gas ring and a machine that cooks rice by itself. She says the rice is fine and the fire is boring.

title: Warmer Winters
paragraphs: My grandfather says that when he was a boy, the pond behind the village froze hard enough to walk on.
It has not frozen like that since 1998. Now it freezes for a week at most, and only near the edge.
This is not a memory problem. Weather records from three stations near his village show the same thing.
The average winter temperature there has gone up by about one and a half degrees in sixty years.

Our teacher says the hole is from 1987, when everyone wrote with a pen you had to fill.
We have a screen on the wall now, and the desks are plastic. But this one desk was too heavy to throw out.
Somebody has carved a date in the corner: 1993. Below it, in new pencil, another student has written 2026.

title: Paper Before Paper
paragraphs: Before paper, Chinese officials wrote on strips of bamboo. One book could fill a cart.
Bamboo is heavy and hard to bend. Silk is light and very expensive, so it was used for small things only.
Paper changed the size of what a person could carry. A whole library became the weight of a bag.
That is why paper is not just a material. It is one of the reasons ideas could travel.
Cheap paper made cheap books, and cheap books made readers.

title: The Four That Travelled
paragraphs: Compass, paper, printing and gunpowder are called the four great inventions of China.
All four left the country and changed other places more than they changed home.
Gunpowder became guns in Europe. The compass made long sea voyages possible. Paper and printing made books cheap enough to argue with.
The inventions were Chinese. The changes they caused were worldwide, and that is a strange and interesting fact.

title: The Compass at Sea
paragraphs: A compass needle points north because the earth itself is a great magnet.
Chinese sailors used a floating needle on water long before ships sailed across open ocean.
Before the compass, sailors followed the coast and the stars. In cloudy weather, they stopped.
With a compass they could cross water they could not see across, and the map of the world got bigger.
A needle in a bowl of water is a small thing. It moved the edge of the known world.

title: One Block, One Page
paragraphs: Woodblock printing works like this: you cut the characters backwards into a flat block of wood, ink it, and press paper on it.
One block prints one page, as many times as you like. A book of two hundred pages needs two hundred blocks.
It sounds slow, and it was, but it was faster and cheaper than copying by hand.
Moveable type came later. In China it was less useful, because written Chinese has thousands of characters and each one needs its own piece.

title: Gunpowder Went Far
paragraphs: Gunpowder was found by people looking for a medicine that would let them live forever.
Instead they got a powder that burns very fast and makes a great deal of gas. In a closed tube, that gas pushes.
Fireworks came first, then weapons. The knowledge moved west along trade routes and changed wars everywhere.
It is a good example of an invention that nobody planned. The inventors were wrong about what they had found.

title: Cai Lun and the Cheap Sheet
paragraphs: In 105, an official named Cai Lun brought the emperor a kind of paper made from tree bark, old cloth and fish nets.
The materials were the point. They were rubbish, and rubbish is cheap and everywhere.
Earlier paper had been made, but from better materials, so it cost too much to use for ordinary writing.
The court accepted the new paper, and within a hundred years it was used for letters, contracts and school books.

title: The Bicycle's Slow Start
paragraphs: The first bicycle had no pedals. You sat on it and pushed your feet against the ground, like a child on a toy.
Then someone put pedals on the front wheel, which made the wheel bigger and bigger until the rider sat two metres up.
The chain fixed that. Two wheels of the same size, a chain, and the risk of falling went down.
It took about eighty years to get from pushing to pedalling, and nobody wrote the plan down in advance.

title: A Machine That Saves Time
paragraphs: A washing machine does in one hour what took a person three hours with a board and a basin.
But it did not only save time. It changed who did the work, and how much water a family used.
Early machines were dangerous. Clothes went through rollers, and hands sometimes went with them.
The modern machine is safe, boring, and completely unnoticed. That is usually what success looks like.

title: The Invention Nobody Notices
paragraphs: A screw is a small, cheap, ordinary thing, and it holds most of the modern world together.
The idea is a slope wrapped around a cylinder. A long gentle slope lets you push something in with little force.
Screws are in your chair, your phone, your door and the plane you flew in last summer.
Nobody has ever said, what a wonderful screw. Inventions that work perfectly become invisible very quickly.

title: My Grandfather's Radio
paragraphs: My grandfather's radio is a wooden box the size of a shoebox, with a cloth over the speaker and two round knobs.
In 1978 it was the only way to hear news in his village. Twenty people sat in his room at eight o'clock.
You turned one knob for the station and one for the volume, and you turned them slowly, or you lost the signal.
It still works. Last week we found a station playing opera, and he sat down and listened for an hour without speaking.

title: Inventions That Failed Well
paragraphs: Some inventions succeed at something other than what they were made for.
A glue that was too weak to hold parts became the sticky note on your desk.
A medicine that did not cure anything became a drink that people still buy a hundred years later.
The lesson is not that failure is good. The lesson is that a failure has to be looked at carefully before it is thrown away.
Most failures are early, not wrong.

title: What We Might Invent Next

The inventions that will matter in fifty years are probably being made now in small rooms by people nobody has heard of.
Some will be about energy, because everything else depends on it. Some will be about water, for the same reason.

title: The First Morning
paragraphs: The first morning of middle school is strange. The building is bigger than my old school, and I do not know a single person in the corridor.
I find my classroom and choose a seat near the window. A girl sits down next to me and says, Hello, I am Lin Yue. What is your name?
That one question opens everything. We talk for twenty minutes about teachers we both know, and about a shop outside the school gate.
By the time the bell rings, I am not nervous any more. One question was enough. Her name is Lin Yue, and now I know three people in this room.

title: Ways to Say Hello
paragraphs: In English, hello is only the beginning. There are many ways to greet a person, and each one tells you something about the situation.
Hello and hi are neutral. You can use them with anyone. Hi is a little more casual, so students use it with friends and teachers who are relaxed.
Nice to meet you is used only the first time. The second time, you say nice to see you again. Mixing these two is a common mistake.
So a greeting is a small piece of social information. It says how close you are, what time it is, and whether this is the first meeting.

title: What I Say About Myself
paragraphs: When I introduce myself, I use four sentences. My name is Chen Hao. I am twelve years old. I am from Guangzhou. I like basketball.
My teacher says this is a good pattern because it is short and clear. But I notice that everybody gives the same four sentences.
The four sentences tell people who I am. The fifth sentence gives them something to ask about. That is the difference.
Now when I meet someone new, I still say the four sentences first. Then I wait. If they ask about the dog, we are going to be friends.

title: Names in English and Chinese
paragraphs: Chinese names put the family name first. English names put the given name first. This is the first thing to get right.
My name is Wang Mei. Wang is my family name and Mei is my given name. In English I write Mei Wang, and people call me Mei.
When you speak to a classmate, use the given name. Using the family name sounds distant, and using the full name sounds like a teacher calling the roll.
So a name carries two things at once: who you are, and how close the other person is allowed to be.

title: Saying Goodbye

title: My Desk
paragraphs: My desk has three zones. The left side is for books, the right side is for the things I use every hour, and the middle is empty.
The middle being empty is the important part. If I put a pen there, I will lose it in two days. If the space is clear, I always know where to look.
The left side holds textbooks, standing up, with the spine facing out. I can find any book without lifting one.
This system takes ten minutes to set up and thirty seconds a day to keep. Before I had it, I spent five minutes every morning looking for my maths book.

title: Where Things Are
paragraphs: English uses three main words for position: in, on and under. They are small, but they carry most of the information.
In means inside something with a boundary. The pen is in the bag. The book is in the drawer. The cat is in the box.
There are two more you will need. Next to means beside, and between means in the middle of two things.
If you can use these five words, you can describe any classroom in the world. That is a lot of power for five short words.

title: The Lost Pencil Case
paragraphs: On Monday I lost my pencil case. I looked in my bag, on my desk and under my chair. It was not there.
I asked the boy behind me. He said he had not seen it. I asked the girl next to me. She said the same thing.
The strange part is this: nothing was missing. The pens, the ruler, the eraser were all inside. Only the position had changed.
I put a label on it that afternoon. A name does not stop you from losing a thing, but it does help the person who finds it.

title: What Is in My School Bag
paragraphs: My school bag weighs about four kilos. Last week I emptied it on the floor to see why.
There were six textbooks, two notebooks, a pencil case, a water bottle and a lunch box. That is the normal part.
I took out everything I had not used in two weeks. The bag went down to two and a half kilos.
A heavy bag is not always a sign of hard work. Sometimes it is just a sign that nobody has looked inside it for a month.
I emptied mine on the floor once. Half of it went into the bin, and I did not miss any of it.

title: A Place for Everything
paragraphs: Mum: Your room is a mess again. Where are your sports shoes?

Mum: Which one? Go and look, please.
Tom: (after a minute) They are in the box. But only one of them.

title: The Map at the Gate
paragraphs: There is a map of the school next to the main gate. Most students walk past it every day and never look at it.
The map shows four teaching buildings, a library, a dining hall, a playground and two gardens. The buildings are numbered, not named.
The map also shows the fire exits. In an emergency, that is the most important information on it.
On my first day, I stood in front of that map for five minutes. Now I could draw it from memory. That is what a school becomes after a few months.

title: Welcome to Our School
paragraphs: Last Friday some primary school students came to visit. I was one of the guides.
I showed them the library first, because it is the quietest place and they were very noisy. Then the playground, because they needed to run.
Another girl asked whether the teachers were strict. I said some are, but not the way you think. They are strict about time, not about hair.
At the end they said thank you and went back to their school. I stood at the gate and remembered that I had asked the same questions a year ago.

title: Places in a School
paragraphs: Every school has the same basic places, and each one has a rule that students learn without being told.
The classroom is for lessons. You speak when the teacher invites you to. The library is for reading. You speak in a low voice, or not at all.
The office is for problems. You knock first, and you say what you need in one sentence.
The rule behind all these rules is the same: a place tells you how to behave. Learn the place, and you learn the manners.

title: The Garden Behind the Library
paragraphs: Behind the library there is a small garden that nobody uses. It has four benches, a lot of grass and one tree.
I found it in October, when I was looking for a place to read. It was quiet, and the tree made shade in the afternoon.
A teacher told us that the garden used to be a car park. Somebody planted the tree thirty years ago, and after that nobody wanted to cut it down.
I like that. A place changed because one person would not remove one tree.

title: First Day, Second Time
paragraphs: This year I helped with the first day of school. I stood at the gate with a sign and answered questions.
A boy came up and asked where Class Seven was. I told him, and then I saw his face. He was not listening. He was looking at the crowd.
He said thank you at the door and went in. I do not know if he remembered any of it.
But I remembered my own first day, and how one person walking with me made the building smaller.
So I walked over and said, I am new too. It was not true. It worked anyway.

title: The Friend I Did Not Choose
paragraphs: The teacher put me next to Zhou Yang in September. We did not choose each other. We were simply given the same desk.
For two weeks we said almost nothing. He drew cars in the corner of his notebook. I read. We shared a ruler when one of us forgot.
I still do not care about engines. But I liked how much he cared. That was the beginning.
Two years later he is the person I call first. We were not matched by interest. We were matched by a seating plan, and then by time.

title: What Makes a Friend
paragraphs: People say a friend is someone who helps you. That is true, but it is not complete. A stranger can help you too.
A friend is someone who knows what you are like when you are not being polite. That takes time, and it takes being seen in bad moments.
And a friend is someone who tells you the truth, but not all of it at once. Timing is part of honesty.
So friendship is not a feeling that arrives. It is a record of small things: shared desks, borrowed rulers, and days when nothing happened.

title: My Best Friend and I
paragraphs: My best friend and I are almost opposites. She talks to everyone. I talk to four people. She decides in a minute. I decide in a week.
This should be a problem, and sometimes it is. She makes plans I do not want. I say nothing, and then she is angry that I said nothing.
Our rule is simple: if one of us says I really do not want to, the other one stops asking. No explanation needed.
That rule took two years to build. It is worth more than the things we have in common.

title: A Letter to a New Classmate
paragraphs: Dear New Classmate,
Welcome to Class Three. I am the person who sits by the door, so you will probably meet me first. Here is what nobody tells you.
Mr Huang checks homework on Monday, so do it on Sunday night, not Monday morning. The PE teacher does not care about speed, only about trying.
You do not have to make friends in the first week. Most of us were alone in September. It sorts itself out by October.
If you get lost, ask anyone. Nobody here minds.
Yours, Chen Yu

title: Names and Nicknames
paragraphs: In my class, almost everybody has two names. The one on the register, and the one people actually use.
Nicknames come from three places. Some come from a physical habit: the boy who always taps his pen is called Drummer.
Some come from a mistake. My friend wrote his name wrong on a test in Grade Five, and the wrong version has followed him ever since.
A nickname is not always kind, but it is always a kind of attention. When a class stops making nicknames for you, that is when you should worry.

title: Four People and One Kitchen
paragraphs: There are four people in my family, and one kitchen. The kitchen is where everything happens.
My father cooks on weekdays because he gets home first. My mother cooks on Sunday because she says he uses too much oil.
I set the table. I have done it since I was seven, so I do it without thinking. Four bowls, four pairs of chopsticks, one small dish of chilli.
Nobody in my family talks about love. They cook, they set the table, they say eat more. That is the same sentence, said differently.

title: The Family Photo on the Wall
paragraphs: There is a photo on our wall of eleven people. I know nine of them. The other two died before I was born.
My grandmother can name everyone, and she can tell you the year and the reason for the photo. It was taken at my uncle's wedding.
I look at the photo sometimes when I am bored. Everybody is standing very straight, nobody is smiling, and everybody is wearing their best clothes.
It is strange to think that one day I will be the person explaining this photo to someone who was not born yet.

title: Words for Family
paragraphs: English family words are much less exact than Chinese ones. This causes real confusion for students.
In Chinese, your father's brother and your mother's brother have different names. In English, both are uncle.
If the detail matters, English adds words: my cousin on my mother's side, my older cousin. It takes longer, but it is clear.
This is a good example of a general rule: a language is exact where its speakers need to be exact, and vague everywhere else.

title: My Grandfather's Shop
paragraphs: My grandfather ran a small shop for thirty-eight years. It sold oil, salt, soap, batteries and newspapers.
He opened at six and closed at nine. He knew every family on the street, and he knew what they would buy before they asked.
He retired last year. The shop is a laundry now.
I asked him once if he was sad. He said, no. Thirty-eight years is a long time to stand in one place. Then he asked me about my exams.
I did not answer. I was thinking about thirty-eight years, and about the day he would lock the door for the last time.

title: Who Does What at Home
paragraphs: Dad: Who washed the dishes last night?
Lily: I did. Tom was supposed to, but he was doing his homework.
Tom: I was doing my homework until ten. Ask Mum.
Mum: He was. But Lily, you cooked, so Tom should wash tonight.
Tom: Fine. But then Lily takes out the rubbish for a week.
Lily: Two days. Dad: Enough, both of you. Write it on the board so we stop having this conversation every morning.
Tom: And who bought the board? Lily: Nobody. It is the back of an old poster.

title: The Library Rule
paragraphs: Our library has one rule that is not written anywhere: the third floor is for silence, the second floor is for group work.
Nobody told me this. I learned it in my first week, by sitting on the third floor with two friends and being looked at.
I have used that system ever since. When I need to think, I go up. When I need to talk, I go down.
Good buildings do this. They do not need signs for everything, because the people inside them agree on how to use the space.

title: A Day of Rooms
paragraphs: A school day is really a tour of rooms, and each room changes how you behave.
You start in the classroom, where you sit in the same seat and speak when called. Then you move to the lab, where you stand, touch things and follow safety rules.
In the afternoon you might go to the art room, where being wrong is allowed, or the music room, where being loud is required.
By four o'clock you have been six different people. This is one reason school is tiring: it is not one place, it is seven.

title: The New Building
paragraphs: Our school opened a new building in September. It has four floors, a lift and a roof garden.
At first everybody wanted to have a lesson there. After a month, nobody did, because the lift broke and the stairs are steep.
Only Class Eight is allowed up there, because their teacher is in charge of the plants. Everybody else complains about this.
I think the complaining is fair. But I also think a school should have one place that is not for everybody. It gives people something to work towards.

title: Directions Inside a Building
paragraphs: Giving directions inside a building needs three kinds of words: position, movement and landmark.
Position words tell you where something is: on the left, on the right, at the end of the corridor, next to the stairs.
A good direction uses all three in one sentence: Go straight, turn left at the notice board, and it is the second door on the right.
If someone still gets lost, the direction was probably too long, not too short. Two short directions beat one perfect one.

title: The Corner Nobody Uses
paragraphs: On the second floor, between the science lab and the stairs, there is a corner with two chairs and a window.
Nobody uses it because it is not a room. It is just space. Teachers walk past it. Students walk past it.
I started sitting there in November, when I needed to finish a project and the classroom was too loud.
Now three other people sit there too. We never arranged it. We just all found the same corner.
A school is designed by adults, but it is used by students. The best places are usually the ones the designers forgot.

title: Why I Like Maths
paragraphs: People assume I like maths because I am good at it. That is backwards. I am good at it because I like it.
What I like is the moment when a problem that looked impossible becomes simple. Not the answer, the moment.
That experience is addictive. You cannot get it from a subject where the answer is an opinion.
This is also why I dislike maths sometimes. When I cannot find the trick, there is nothing to say. With a story, you can always write something.

title: The Subject I Am Bad At
paragraphs: I am bad at English listening. Not reading, not writing. Listening.
The problem is speed. When I read, I can go back. When I listen, the sentence is gone before I finish it.
My teacher gave me one piece of advice that worked. She said, stop trying to understand every word. Listen for the verb.
So I did. I listened for what was happening, not for what was said. My score went from sixty to seventy-eight in two months.
I am still not good at it. But I am no longer afraid of it, and that is half the work.

title: A Timetable Tells a Story
paragraphs: A school timetable looks boring. It is actually a set of decisions about what children should know.
Chinese and maths get the morning slots, because those subjects need a clear head. Art and music usually come after lunch.
The number of hours per week is the real message. A subject with one hour a week is a subject the school values but does not prioritise.
So when people argue about education, they often argue about the timetable. It is the one place where beliefs become hours.
