title: The Teacher Who Changed It
paragraphs: I hated history until Grade Seven. The textbook was a list of years and names, and I could not remember any of them.
Then a new teacher arrived. She did not start with the year. She started with a question: what would you have done?
We spent one lesson arguing about whether a farmer should have joined a rebellion. We never opened the book.
At the end she said, now read pages forty to forty-five, and tell me if you still think the same.
I read them twice. That was the first time a history book had ever answered a question I actually had.

title: Choosing Subjects
paragraphs: Student: I have to choose between geography and biology next year.
Teacher: Which one do you think about when nobody asks you to?
Student: Neither. I think about football.
Teacher: All right, different question. Which one do you find easier to remember after the test?
Student: Geography. I still know about the rivers. Biology I forget in a week.
Teacher: Then that is your answer for now. Liking comes later, and it usually comes after you stop feeling lost.

title: The Club I Joined by Accident
paragraphs: I went to the wrong room on club day. I was looking for the basketball club and found the debating club.
A girl handed me a piece of paper and said, you are on the other side. I did not know what the other side was.
Twenty minutes later I was arguing that homework should be banned. I lost, badly, and I enjoyed it.
I never went back to basketball. I have been in the debating club for two years now.
My mother still tells people I joined by accident. I tell her that most good things start as mistakes.

title: What a Club Gives You
paragraphs: A club is not a lesson. Nobody grades you, and nobody makes you attend. That is exactly why it works.
First, it gives you a reason to be somewhere after school. This sounds small, but a reason is what keeps a Person from going home to a screen.
Third, it gives you a job. Somebody has to bring the equipment, keep the time, write the notice. That is where responsibility actually comes from.
So a school without clubs is only half a school. It teaches subjects but not belonging.

title: The Poster
paragraphs: Our club needed members, so we made a poster. The first version failed completely.
It had a long paragraph explaining what we do. Nobody read it. People look at posters for about two seconds.
We learned four rules. Use fewer words. Use one picture that shows an action, not a group standing still. Put the time and place at the bottom, where the eye ends.
And put the poster where people wait, not where they walk. A queue is a reading opportunity. A corridor is not.

title: Joining the Film Club
paragraphs: Amy: Are you coming to the film club on Wednesday?
Ben: What do you do there? Just watch films?
Amy: We watch one scene, then we talk about how it was made. Last week we looked at a chase scene for forty minutes.
Ben: Forty minutes for one scene?
Amy: It was one shot. No cuts. The camera follows the car for three minutes without stopping.
Ben: All right, that sounds interesting. What time? Amy: Four thirty, Room 205. Bring nothing.
Ben: Nothing? Amy: Nothing. Just yourself.

title: The Club That Ended
paragraphs: Our photography club closed last term. There were eleven members in September and three in December.
The reason was simple. The club met on Friday afternoon, and Friday afternoon is when everybody has something else.
The teacher tried to move it to Wednesday. By then the three remaining members had joined other clubs.
I think about this sometimes. The club did not fail because nobody liked photography. It failed because of a timetable.
Good ideas die of small practical things far more often than of bad ideas.

unit: Unit 6 A Day in the Life
title: Six Twenty
paragraphs: I get up at six twenty. Not six fifteen, not six thirty. Six twenty, because that is when the alarm that actually works goes off.
There are three alarms on my phone. The first one at six o'clock I turn off without waking up. The second at six ten I snooze. The third at six twenty I obey.
The walk to school takes twelve minutes if I go the short way, eighteen if I go past the shop. I go past the shop on Fridays.
People ask why I do not get up earlier. I have tried. Getting up earlier just means snoozing longer.

unit: Unit 6 A Day in the Life
title: Why Teenagers Sleep Late
paragraphs: Parents often say teenagers are lazy in the morning. Science says something different.
During the teenage years, the body clock shifts later by about two hours. The hormone that makes you sleepy is released later at night.
The problem is that school starts at the same time as before. The result is a permanent small sleep debt during the week.
This is why many doctors suggest later start times for secondary schools. It is not about comfort. It is about attention, mood and memory.

unit: Unit 6 A Day in the Life
title: The Hour After School
paragraphs: The hour between four and five is the most dangerous hour of my day.
I come home, put down my bag, and sit on the bed for a minute. That minute becomes forty.
By the time I stand up, I am tired, and the homework has grown in my head until it looks impossible.
So I made a rule. I do not sit down before I have done one small thing. Not all the homework. One thing.
Usually one thing turns into three. The trick is not discipline. The trick is not sitting down.

unit: Unit 6 A Day in the Life
title: A Day in Two Countries
paragraphs: A student's day in China and a student's day in Britain have the same length but a different shape.
In China, the day usually starts early, around seven thirty, and ends around five. There is a long lunch break and often a nap.
The biggest difference is the evening. British students often have sports or clubs after school. Chinese students often have homework until nine or ten.
Neither shape is naturally better. Each one fits a different set of expectations about what school is for.

title: Sunday Evening
paragraphs: Sunday evening has its own feeling. It starts at about six, when the light goes and you remember tomorrow.
I check my bag. Books for the first four lessons, the maths worksheet, the PE shirt. Then I check again, because the first check does not count.
At nine I stop working, whether or not I have finished. This is a rule I made after a term of sleeping at midnight.
The unfinished part gets done at lunch on Monday. It always does. The panic, on the other hand, never helped.

title: The Birthday I Remember
paragraphs: The birthday I remember best was the one when nothing went right.
The cake fell on the way home. The restaurant was full. Two friends could not come because of a football match.
So we sat on the floor of my room with a broken cake, four people instead of eight, and ate it with spoons.
Somebody started telling stories about primary school. We laughed until my mother knocked on the door.
I have had better-planned birthdays. I do not remember any of them. What I remember is the year the plan collapsed and we stayed anyway.

title: Why We Have Birthdays
paragraphs: A birthday marks a day that is not special in any natural way. The earth does not notice it.
Its meaning is entirely social. It says: we are glad you exist, and we are counting.
The counting is the interesting part. For a child, a birthday is a gain. For an older person, it can feel like a subtraction.
So the same date carries opposite meanings depending on where you are in life. This is why birthday wishes are careful.
In the end, a birthday is a yearly reminder that other people are keeping track of you. That is worth a cake.

title: Dates and Ordinal Numbers
paragraphs: Talking about birthdays requires two things that Chinese speakers often mix up: months and ordinal numbers.
There are twelve months. In English they are always written with a capital letter, and they are never numbered in speech.
The pattern for ordinals is regular except for the first three and the ones ending in them: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, then 4th to 20th all take th.
A common mistake is saying May one. It is understood, but it sounds like a page number, not a date.
So: on the fifth of May, or on May the fifth. Both are right. May five is not.

title: The Present I Did Not Want
paragraphs: For my twelfth birthday, my aunt gave me a dictionary. A large one. It weighed more than my school bag.
I said thank you and put it on the shelf, where it stayed for a year.
Then in Grade Seven I started writing English compositions and could not find the right word. Every time, I went to that dictionary.
It turned out to be the most useful present I have ever received. I have never told my aunt this.
I should. A present that looks wrong at first can be right for years. That is a thing worth saying out loud.

I asked the guard about him. He said the dog belongs to a family on the fourth floor. They moved in two years ago.
Nobody trained him to do this. He simply decided that the gate is where the family comes back.

title: Why Some Animals Live in Groups
paragraphs: Many animals live in groups, and the reason is usually one of three: safety, food, or warmth.
Safety comes first. A single small animal is easy to catch. In a group, somebody is always watching while the others eat or sleep.
Warmth matters for animals in cold places. Penguins stand close together and take turns on the outside of the group.
So a group is not just company. It is a survival tool, and most animals that live alone have some other protection.

title: The Elephant's Memory
paragraphs: People say elephants never forget. This is not a joke; there is evidence behind it.
In one study, researchers played recordings of three groups of elephants. One group was friendly, one was unknown, one had attacked the herd before.
The recordings were made years earlier. Some of the elephants that heard them had never met the ones in the recording.
So the knowledge had passed through the group. Memory, for an elephant, is not only personal. It is also something a family keeps.

title: A Cat and a Bird
paragraphs: My aunt has a cat and a bird. Everybody said this would end badly, and for two weeks it looked likely.
The cat sat under the cage for hours. The bird made a noise every time the cat moved.
The cat looked up, yawned, and went to sleep. He had never actually wanted the bird. He wanted the cage, which was warm.
They have lived together for six years now. The bird sometimes walks on the cat's back. Neither of them finds this strange.
The cat is old and slow. The bird is bold. It works.

title: Should We Keep Wild Animals?
paragraphs: Some people say zoos protect endangered animals. Others say a zoo is a prison with a good story.
Both are partly right. A good zoo can breed animals that would die outside, and it can teach children things a book cannot.
So the question is not whether zoos are good or bad. The question is what standard we accept.
My own view is simple. If the animal can be returned to the wild, the zoo is doing a job. If it can only live in the cage, we are keeping it for ourselves.

title: The Rule Nobody Likes
paragraphs: Our school does not allow phones during the day. Every student complains about this, including me.
The rule works like this: phones go into a box at eight o'clock and come out at four. The box is in the classroom, not in the office.
By the third week, the corridor was louder and the classroom was calmer. I noticed because I could hear the difference.
I still do not like the rule. But I have stopped saying it is useless, because I can see what it changed.

title: Why Rules Need Reasons
paragraphs: A rule without a reason lasts until the person in charge leaves the room.
If a teacher says, do not run in the corridor, students will run when the teacher is not there. If the teacher says, the floor is wet and people fall, the rule travels with them.
There is a second condition. The rule should apply to everyone, including the person who made it.
A rule that only binds the young is not a rule. It is a demand, and demands are obeyed only while somebody is watching.

title: Signs and What They Mean
paragraphs: Public signs are a short form of writing, and they work in a particular way.
Most signs use the imperative: Stop. No Entry. Keep Off the Grass. The verb comes first because the reader may be walking past.
Some signs give information rather than orders: Exit, Push, Emergency Phone. These are read in a hurry, so they are always short.
The test of a good sign is whether a stranger can understand it in one second. If it needs a second reading, it is badly made.

title: The Rule That Was Cancelled
paragraphs: Last term our class had a rule: no food in the classroom. It was made after an ant problem.
In November somebody pointed out that the rule also banned water. Students were going six hours without drinking.
We wrote a proposal to the class teacher. It had three points: water in a closed bottle, no other drinks, no food.
She accepted it in one day. The new rule is on the wall with the date and the reason.
What I learned is that a rule can be argued with. You need a proposal, not a complaint.

title: Traffic Rules in Two Cities
paragraphs: Traffic rules look the same everywhere, but the way people follow them is not.
In Guangzhou, most people wait for the green light even when the road is empty. In some smaller cities, people cross whenever there is a gap.
There is also a design factor. A crossing with a countdown timer is followed better than one without, because people know how long they must wait.
So order is not created by writing rules. It is created by making the rule easy to follow and hard to ignore.

title: Running in the Morning
paragraphs: I started running in March because I could not climb four floors without stopping.
The first week I ran for three minutes and walked for seven. I did this four times a week.
By May I could run for fifteen minutes without stopping. Nothing dramatic happened. My legs simply stopped complaining.
The change I noticed most was not fitness. It was sleep. I began falling asleep at eleven instead of one.
I still do not enjoy running. I enjoy having run. That is a different thing, and it is enough.

title: How Much Exercise Is Enough
paragraphs: Doctors usually recommend one hour of activity a day for children and teenagers. That sounds like a lot.
But the hour does not have to be sport. Walking to school counts. Climbing stairs counts. PE lessons count.
What matters is the heart rate. Activity that makes you breathe faster for ten minutes or more is the kind that helps.
Strength matters too, but less for young people. Two sessions a week of climbing, carrying or jumping is enough.
So the target is not an hour of training. It is an hour of not sitting still, spread across the day.

title: The Football Team
paragraphs: Our class football team lost every match in Grade Seven. Nine matches, nine losses.
The problem was not skill. Two of our players were the best in the year. The problem was that nobody passed.
We lost the first two matches and drew the third. Then something changed. We started winning, not because we were better, but because we were together.
We came third that year. I still think the rule about three touches was the whole season.
Three touches, then pass. It sounded simple, and it changed the whole season.

title: Sleep Is Part of Training
paragraphs: Athletes train hard and sleep harder. Most of them sleep nine or ten hours, and they treat it as a session, not a rest.
The reason is that the body repairs itself during deep sleep. Muscle grows at night, not in the gym.
Students who train and sleep six hours are doing half the work. They also get injured more often.
The same is true for the brain. What you study in the evening is sorted and stored while you sleep.
So staying up to revise is a bad trade. You gain one hour and lose the process that makes the hour useful.

title: Joining the Swimming Club
paragraphs: Coach: Can you swim already? Ben: I can, but not well. Twenty metres, maybe.
Coach: That is enough to start. We train Tuesday and Thursday, five to six thirty.
Ben: I have a maths class on Thursday. Coach: Then come on Saturday morning instead. Same session, different day.
Ben: Do I need to buy anything? Coach: A cap and goggles. We have spare ones for the first month.
Ben: All right, I will come on Tuesday. Coach: Good. Bring a water bottle and do not eat for an hour before.

title: Why I Stopped Playing Basketball
paragraphs: I played basketball for four years and stopped at fourteen. People assume I was injured. I was not.
The reason was simpler. I was not good enough to enjoy it any more. When everybody around you improves faster, the game stops being fun.
Two years later I went back to basketball for a school match. I was still slow. But I could watch the game properly, and that was new.
Sometimes quitting a thing is not giving up. It is changing what you want from it.

title: Breakfast
paragraphs: Breakfast is the meal students skip most often, and it is the one that matters most before a school day.
After eight hours without food, blood sugar is low. The brain runs on glucose, so attention and mood both drop.
Sweet drinks and cakes give a fast rise and a fast fall. Students who eat only that are hungry again by ten.
Ten minutes is enough time to eat properly. The problem is usually not time. It is that nobody got up ten minutes earlier. That small choice changes the morning.

title: The Canteen Menu
paragraphs: Our canteen changed its menu in September. The old one had fried chicken every day. The new one has it twice a week.
Students complained for two weeks. Then they stopped, because the queue for the noodle counter got longer and the fried food counter got shorter.
He also said something I did not expect. He said the students eat what is easy to reach. So he moved the fruit bowl to the front.
Fruit sales tripled in a month. Nobody gave a lecture about health. Somebody moved a bowl.

title: Food Words in English
paragraphs: Talking about food in English needs three kinds of words, and students often learn only the first.
The first is the name of the food: rice, noodles, pork, cabbage. These are easy and there are many of them.
The second is the way it is cooked: fried, boiled, steamed, roasted, stir-fried. One food can have five names.
The third is the amount: a bowl of, a plate of, a slice of, a spoonful of. English counts food by container, not by piece.
This is why a bowl of rice sounds natural and a rice sounds wrong. The container is part of the word.

title: My Grandmother's Soup
paragraphs: My grandmother makes soup every Sunday. The recipe has never been written down.
I asked her for it once. She said, some pork, some ginger, and whatever is in the fridge. That was the whole recipe.
Then everything goes into a pot with fresh water for two hours. She never measures. She tastes, twice.
I have tried to copy it four times. It is always close and never the same. I have decided that is the recipe.
The soup takes four hours and a whole afternoon of standing by the stove. She says the waiting is the secret. I believe her.

title: Ordering in a Restaurant
paragraphs: Waiter: Are you ready to order? Amy: Yes. Do you have anything without meat?
Waiter: The tofu with mushrooms, and the green beans. Both are vegetarian.
Amy: I will have the tofu. And a bowl of rice, please.
Ben: I will have the chicken. Is it very hot? Waiter: Mild. You can ask for less chilli.
Ben: Then less chilli, please. Waiter: Anything to drink? Amy: Two glasses of water.
Amy: Could we have the bill, please? Waiter: Together or separate? Ben: Together. I am paying.
Amy: No, you paid last time. Waiter: I will leave it with you.

title: Why Diets Fail
paragraphs: Most diets fail, and the reason is not weak willpower. It is that a diet is a temporary rule applied to a permanent habit.
If you eat differently for six weeks and then stop, the old pattern comes back in a month. Nothing has actually changed.
The plans that work are boring. They change one thing: fewer sweet drinks, or a smaller bowl, or fruit instead of biscuits.
One change is easy to keep. Ten changes are a project, and projects end.
So the question is not what to give up. It is what you can still be doing in two years.

title: What Is Happening Now
paragraphs: English has a tense for things happening at this moment: the present continuous. It is built with be plus ing.
The form is simple, but the meaning needs care. It describes an action in progress, not a habit.
Some verbs rarely take this form. Know, want, like and believe describe states, not actions. Saying I am knowing is wrong.
There is one more use. It can describe a temporary situation: I am staying at my aunt's this week. Next week, I will be home.
So the tense is not only about now. It is about anything that is still open.

title: A Photograph of a Street
paragraphs: Look at this photograph. It was taken at six in the evening on a Friday.
In the middle, a man is carrying two bags of vegetables. He is looking at his phone.
On the left, three students are waiting for a bus. One of them is eating something from a paper bag.
In the background, a woman is closing her shop. She is pulling down the metal door with one hand.
Nobody in the photograph is doing anything important. That is why I like it. It is just a street, being a street.

title: While I Was Walking Home
paragraphs: While I was walking home yesterday, it started to rain. I had no umbrella, so I stood under a tree.
Two boys were playing football in the car park. They kept playing until the ball was too wet to kick.
A woman was waiting at the bus stop, holding a newspaper over her head. She was laughing at herself.
Then the rain stopped as suddenly as it began, and everybody came out from under their trees and doors.
The whole thing lasted eight minutes. Nobody will remember it except the people who were standing there.

title: The Street at Seven
paragraphs: At seven in the morning, the street is doing four things at once.
The noodle shop is opening. The owner is carrying out a table and stacking stools against the wall.
The crossing is filling up. People are walking quickly, and nobody is looking at anybody else.
The school gate is the busiest place. Parents are stopping their cars, children are getting out, and a guard is waving everybody forward.
By half past seven it is over. The street is empty again, and the shops are open, waiting for the next rush.

title: On the Phone
paragraphs: Mum: Where are you? I am standing at the gate.
Tom: I am still in the classroom. We are finishing a project.
Mum: All right. I am going to the shop. Call me when you come down.
Tom: Wait, Mum. It is raining here. Are you carrying an umbrella? Mum: Yes. Two, actually.
Tom: All right. I will be down in fifteen. Mum: And do not run on the stairs, it is wet.
Tom: I will not. Mum: You said that last week. Tom: And I did not run last week.
Mum: True. See you in fifteen.

title: The City Is Changing
paragraphs: My grandfather says the city he grew up in no longer exists. He does not mean it was destroyed. He means it was replaced.
The market where he worked is now a shopping centre. The river he swam in is now a road with railings on both sides.
What is lost is not the buildings. It is the knowledge of how people used to live there.
So when a neighbourhood is rebuilt, somebody should write down what was there. Not to stop the change, but to keep the record.

title: The Typhoon Day
paragraphs: The typhoon was announced on Tuesday. School closed on Wednesday, and everybody was happy about it until the power went out.
By ten in the morning the wind was hitting the windows in bursts. We put towels along the bottom of the door.
We spent the afternoon moving books onto chairs. My father held a torch while my mother cooked on a gas ring.
The next morning the sky was clean and blue. The street was full of branches. It looked like nothing had happened.

title: Why It Rains
paragraphs: Rain begins with evaporation. The sun heats water in the sea, the rivers and the soil, and some of it turns into vapour.
Warm air rises, carrying the vapour with it. As it rises, it cools. Cool air cannot hold as much water.
Inside the cloud the droplets bump into each other and join. When one is heavy enough, it falls.
If the air below is very cold, it falls as snow. If it passes through a warm layer and then a cold one, it falls as hail.
So rain is not water falling from nowhere. It is water going up, and then coming back down.

title: Four Seasons in One City
paragraphs: Guangzhou has four seasons on paper, but the paper is optimistic.
Spring is warm and wet. The walls sweat, clothes do not dry, and everything smells of damp for about six weeks.
Winter is mild and grey. It rarely goes below ten degrees, but there is no heating indoors, so it feels colder than the number says.
So the year is really two seasons and two short transitions. The calendar says four because calendars are made for the whole country. Here, the weather has its own schedule.

title: What to Wear
paragraphs: Amy: What is the weather like in Beijing in October?
Ben: Cold in the morning, warm at noon. About eight degrees at seven, and twenty at two.
Amy: So what do I wear? Ben: A T-shirt and a jacket. You will take the jacket off by eleven.
Amy: And at night? Ben: Colder than you expect. Bring something warmer than you think you need.
Amy: Should I bring an umbrella? Ben: Yes. It does not rain often, but when it does it is cold rain.
Amy: And a hat. Ben: Now you sound like my mother.

title: The Weather and My Mood
paragraphs: People say rain makes them sad. I think it is more exact than that: rain makes people stay in, and staying in makes some people sad.
The weather itself does very little. What changes is what we do. A rainy day cancels a football match and leaves an afternoon empty.
This matters because it gives us a choice. If the problem is the empty afternoon, the answer is a plan, not sunshine.
I keep a list of things to do on rainy days. It is a short list, and it has never failed.

title: Before the Storm
paragraphs: There is a moment before a summer storm when everything goes still. The wind stops, the birds stop, and the air feels heavy.
Then the temperature drops. You can feel it on your arms before you see anything.
The first drops are large and separate. They hit the dust and make small dark circles.
Then the whole sky arrives at once. The rain is not falling in drops any more; it is falling in sheets.
Ten minutes later it is over. Steam comes off the road. Somebody opens a window, and the whole street smells of wet cement.

title: The Umbrella
paragraphs: I bought an umbrella in June and lost it in July. This happens to me twice a year.
The strange thing is that I never lose anything else. Not my keys, not my wallet. Only umbrellas.
A friend explained it. An umbrella is the only object you carry only when you do not need it visible. It hangs, it gets put down, it stays.
So I bought a very ugly one, bright orange, with a broken handle. I could not leave it anywhere without noticing.
I have had it for fourteen months. It is the longest relationship I have had with an umbrella.

title: The Day I Got Lost
paragraphs: I got lost in Hong Kong when I was nine. It lasted about forty minutes, and it felt like a week.
I was following my father through a market. I stopped to look at a stall selling toys, and when I turned round, he was gone.
After a while a woman in a shop asked if I was alone. She let me sit on a stool inside and gave me water.
My father came back eleven minutes later. He had run three streets. He did not shout at me. He just said, good, you stayed.

title: Why We Remember Some Days
paragraphs: Most days disappear. A few stay for decades. The difference is not how good or bad the day was.
The first factor is novelty. A new route, a new food, a first time doing anything makes the brain record more detail.
The third is story. If a day has a shape, with a beginning and an end, it is easier to keep. That is why we remember the day we got lost but not the day we did homework.
So a memorable day is not necessarily a happy one. It is one that was different, felt strongly, and can be told.

title: The Last Day of Primary School
paragraphs: On the last day of primary school, we were told to clean the classroom. Nobody wanted to, and everybody did it anyway.
We took down the posters and found six years of marks on the wall. Somebody's name was written behind a map in Grade Three.
Mine said: you talk too much in class, and the room is quieter when you are absent. I have thought about that sentence for years.
We left at noon. The gate was the same as always. I remember being surprised that it looked exactly the same.

title: A Trip I Would Do Again
paragraphs: In the summer of Grade Six, my family went to a small town in the north. There was nothing to see there. That was the point.
We stayed four days. We walked the same two streets every morning, ate at the same noodle shop, and sat by the river in the evening.
I have been to bigger places since. I remember very little of them, because we were always moving.
This is what I learned from that trip: four days in one place beats one day in four places. The town was boring, and that is why I remember it.

title: Telling a Story About a Day
paragraphs: Telling a story about a day needs three things: a time order, a turning point and a detail.
Time order is easy. Use first, then, after that, and finally. But do not use all of them; two or three are enough.
The detail is what makes it believable. Not the whole scene, one thing: the colour of a door, the sound of a bell, the price of a ticket.
A story with all three is short and clear. A story with only time order is a list, and nobody remembers a list.

title: The Sports Day
paragraphs: Amy: How was Sports Day? I heard it rained.
Ben: It did, in the morning. The track was wet, so they moved the running to the afternoon.
Amy: That is not bad. Ben: It is not good either. But I did not stop, and that was the goal.
Amy: Was your class happy? Ben: We got second overall. Nobody expected that, so everybody was in a good mood by four o'clock.
Amy: Did you train for it? Ben: Two weeks. Mostly running up and down the stairs at home.
Amy: That explains why you were not last. Ben: That, and the boy who fell at the start.

title: The Woodcutter and the Axe
paragraphs: A woodcutter dropped his axe into the river. He sat on the bank and cried, because it was the only axe he had.
A spirit rose from the water holding a golden axe. Is this yours? she asked. The woodcutter said no.
The spirit was pleased with his honesty and gave him all three.

His neighbour heard the story, dropped his axe in the river on purpose, and when the spirit brought up a golden one, said yes immediately. The spirit went back into the water and left him with nothing.

title: Why Fairy Tales Begin with Once
paragraphs: Almost every fairy tale begins with once upon a time. The phrase does two jobs at the same moment.
First, it removes the story from the calendar. There is no year, so nobody can check whether it happened.
The ending has its own phrase: and they lived happily ever after. Both phrases are promises about the shape of the story.
This is why a fairy tale does not need a realistic setting. The opening has already told you what kind of world you are in.

title: The Three Wishes
paragraphs: A poor man was given three wishes. He went home and told his wife, and they argued about how to use them.
While they argued, he was hungry. He said, without thinking, I wish I had a sausage. A sausage appeared on the plate.
His wife was furious. She said, you wasted a wish on a sausage! I wish the sausage was on your nose!
The sausage jumped onto his nose, and stuck there.
So they used the third wish to get it off. That evening they had nothing but a sausage, and they were laughing too hard to eat it.

title: The Fox and the Crow
paragraphs: A crow found a piece of cheese and sat in a tree to eat it. A fox came and stood under the tree.
The fox said, good morning, beautiful bird. Your feathers are the finest I have seen. Surely your voice must be as fine.
The crow was pleased. She opened her beak to sing, and the cheese fell.
The fox caught it and said, that was all I wanted. Thank you for the lesson: never trust a person who praises you for no reason.
The crow learned something too. She never sang in a tree with food in her mouth again.

title: What Fairy Tales Teach
paragraphs: People say fairy tales are for children. The stories are simple, the good are rewarded, and the wicked are punished.
But the simple shape is doing a serious job. A child meets dishonesty, greed and jealousy for the first time in a story, not in life.
The danger is when the shape becomes a promise: be good and you will be rich. Real life does not work like that, and children discover it soon enough.
So the stories are not instructions. They are rehearsals. We practise judging people in a world where we cannot be harmed.

title: Reading to My Cousin
paragraphs: My cousin is five. She asks me to read the same book every night, and it is a very bad book.
The pictures are ugly and the story makes no sense. A bear steals a bicycle and rides it to the sea. That is the whole plot.
So I read it again, and I started changing things. The bear now has a name, a family and a reason for wanting a bicycle.
She has not noticed. She still thinks it is the same book. I have told the story eleven times and the bear has had four different jobs.

title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
paragraphs: A shepherd boy was bored, so he ran to the village shouting that a wolf had come. The villagers ran up the hill with sticks. There was no wolf.
He did it again the next week. Again they came, and again there was nothing.
The third week a wolf really did come. The boy shouted, and nobody moved.
The villagers heard him. They had heard him before.
The story ends with the sheep, not the boy. This is the part people forget. The cost of a lie is not paid by the liar alone.

title: Three Days in the Mountains
paragraphs: Last summer my family spent three days in a village in the mountains. There was one road, one shop and no phone signal.
The first day I was bored. I had brought two books and finished one by lunchtime. In the afternoon I walked to the end of the road and back.
By the third day I had stopped counting the hours. I was not bored any more; I was simply busy with small things.
On the way home the signal came back on my phone. I looked at it, and then I put it away for another hour.
Three days was enough. A fourth would have been too many.

title: What a Holiday Is For
paragraphs: People describe holidays as a break from work. But most holidays are more tiring than the working week.
We get up early to catch a train, walk for eight hours, take photographs and eat too much. We come home and need a holiday.
The trouble is that a described holiday is not the same as a restful one. They are two different products.
So the useful question before a trip is not where to go, but which of the two you need this time.
The best holidays I remember were cheap ones. Nobody was in a hurry, and each day had only one plan in it.

title: The Holiday I Learned From
paragraphs: When I was eleven, my parents let me plan a two-day trip by myself. It was a small trip, to a town two hours away.
I made three mistakes. I booked a hotel far from the station. I planned four places for one afternoon. I did not check that the museum closed on Mondays.
On the train home my father asked what I would change. I said everything, and he laughed.
Since then I have planned every family trip. I am much better at it, and I still check the opening days first.
That mistake cost us one afternoon. The lesson has saved us about ten.

title: A Postcard Home
paragraphs: Dear Grandma,
We are in a small town by the sea. The hotel is old and the lift does not work, but our room looks onto the water.
Every morning fishermen bring their boats in at about six. I have watched them three times and I still do not understand how the nets work.
The food is very simple: rice, fish, and a soup with a name I cannot pronounce. I have eaten it four days in a row.
We come home on Friday. I will bring you the dried fish you asked for, and a photograph of the boats.
Love, Mei
P.S. The train leaves at seven. Do not be late again.

title: Talking About a Trip
paragraphs: Ben: How was your trip to Xi'an?
Amy: Good, but crowded. The museum was fully booked for three days.
Ben: Did you see the terracotta soldiers? Amy: Yes, we got tickets for the last morning.
Ben: Was it worth it? Amy: It was. I stood in front of them for twenty minutes and said nothing.
Ben: And the food? Amy: Better than the soldiers, honestly. I had noodles four times.
Ben: Would you go again? Amy: In winter, yes. Not in July.
Ben: Noted. Amy: And book the museum a week early. I am serious.
Ben: I will book it tonight. Amy: And set an alarm this time.

title: The Photograph I Did Not Take
paragraphs: There is a photograph I did not take, and I still think about it.
It was in a village in Yunnan. An old woman was sitting on a low wall, mending a basket. Behind her the sun was going down over the fields.
I had my camera in my hand. I raised it, and then I stopped, because she had looked up and seen me.
I asked if I could take a picture. She shook her head and smiled, and went back to the basket.
I have hundreds of photographs from that trip. I remember that one minute better than all of them.
That minute is the clearest thing I brought home.

title: Why We Bring Back Souvenirs
paragraphs: Every tourist shop sells the same three things: a magnet, a key ring and a small model of a famous building.
Nobody needs these objects. They are bought because a holiday feels incomplete without something to carry home.
This is why the ugliest objects are often kept longest. Their value has nothing to do with how they look.
I have a stone from a beach in Fujian. It is a grey stone. It has been on my desk for nine years.
It cost nothing and does nothing. But when I hold it I am on that beach again, with wet shoes and a bag of hot bread.

title: Who Does the Most
paragraphs: In most families, one person does more housework than everybody else, and it is usually not the person who thinks so.
Studies that ask family members to estimate their share find a consistent pattern: almost everyone overestimates their own contribution.
So the argument about housework is rarely about laziness. It is about visibility.
The families that argue least are usually the ones with a written list. A list makes invisible work visible, and then the argument is about facts.
A list works better when everyone writes it than when one person hands it out.

title: The Kitchen Light
paragraphs: In my house, the kitchen light is always on. My mother leaves it on when she goes to bed, in case somebody comes home late.
For years I thought this was carelessness. I turned it off every night and she turned it back on.
Then I went to stay with a friend for a week. His house was dark at midnight, and I found it strange and a little cold.
When I came back, I left the light on myself. Nobody asked me why.
A house is not made of walls. It is made of these small arrangements that only make sense to the people inside.

title: Moving House
paragraphs: We moved when I was twelve. It was four streets away, which sounds small and is not.
The new flat was bigger and brighter. My room had a window facing east, so I woke up early for the first month.
What fixed it was a broken chair. My father repaired it in the new living room, with the same tools and the same complaining.
After that the flat was ours. Home, it turns out, is not the building. It is the set of habits you bring into it.
Two months later I stopped hearing the road, and my mother stopped apologising for the kitchen. That is when a place becomes yours.

title: Rules at Home
paragraphs: Mum: We need to talk about the weekends.
Tom: What about them? Mum: You come home at eleven and nobody knows where you are.
Tom: I am with friends. Mum: I know. I still want a message at nine.
Tom: That is every weekend? Mum: Every weekend. One message, one line. Then I sleep.
Tom: All right. And if I forget? Mum: Then I call you, and you will not like the conversation.
Tom: What if my phone is dead? Mum: Then borrow one. There is always somebody with a phone.
Tom: Fine. Mum: And Tom, nine o clock means nine, not nine thirty.

title: My Grandparents' Village House
paragraphs: My grandparents' house has one room that nobody uses. It is kept exactly as it was when my great-grandmother lived there.
There is a wooden bed, a table, a mirror and a photograph. Nothing has been moved for thirty years.
My grandmother cleans it once a month. She does not sit in it. She opens the window, dusts the table, and closes the door.
I asked her once why she keeps it. She said, because it is still her room.
I did not understand this when I was ten. Now I think it is the most sensible thing in the house.

title: Why Small Flats Feel Bigger
paragraphs: A small flat can feel larger than a big one, and the reason is usually not the area.
The first factor is sight lines. If you can see from the door to the window without a wall in the way, the space reads as one room.
The third is light. A room with one small window feels smaller than the same room with a wide one, because the eye needs an exit.
So the design question is not how many square metres you have. It is how many places your eye can go.
A mirror at the end of a corridor adds three metres that do not exist. So does a window you can see from the door.

title: Two Brothers
paragraphs: My brother and I are two years apart and share a room, a school and most of our friends.
People assume we are similar. We are not. He decides in a minute and regrets it for a week. I decide in a week and never regret it.
The arrangement works because we divided the room without discussing it. He has the window side, I have the wall side.
We also divided the arguments. He is allowed to be angry first. I am allowed to be right later.
This is not a rule anybody wrote down. It took about three years and one broken lamp.

title: Why Difference Is Useful
paragraphs: Groups of similar people are comfortable and weak. This is not an opinion; it is a pattern found in many studies of decision making.
When everyone has the same background, they share the same blind spots. Nobody notices the missing question, because nobody thinks to ask it.
The condition is that the difference must be allowed to speak. A group with one quiet outsider is still a group of similar people.
So the value is not diversity itself. It is disagreement that is safe to express.
A group where nobody dares to disagree is quiet, not peaceful.

title: The New Student
paragraphs: A new student joined our class in October. She had moved from another province and spoke with a different accent.
For two weeks she sat alone at lunch. Not because anybody was unkind, but because nobody had a reason to sit with her.
She was very good at it. She had done the same project at her old school and knew which design would hold the most weight.
By Friday she had four people asking her questions. A project did what two weeks of good intentions could not.
She was not shy. She had simply been given nothing to do for two weeks.

title: Comparing Two Schools
paragraphs: I changed schools in Grade Eight, so I can compare two systems from the inside.
The first school had fifty students in a class and one teacher. The second has thirty-eight and two, for some subjects.
Neither is simply better. The first made me fast and accurate. The second made me better at planning and speaking.
What I noticed most is that both schools believed they were normal. That is what a system does: it makes itself invisible.
At my school one bell rings for everyone at once and nobody finds it strange. Neither system is natural; both are simply old.

title: Agreeing to Disagree
paragraphs: Amy: I think school should start at nine.
Ben: Then it would end at five. I would rather finish at four.
Amy: We could shorten the lunch break. Ben: Lunch is the only hour I am awake.
Amy: That is not true. Ben: It is half true. Look, we agree on the problem.
Amy: Do we? Ben: Yes. Neither of us wants to get up at six thirty.
Amy: All right. Then let us write that down and argue about the solution later.
Ben: Write it down, then. Amy: Problem: nobody wants to get up at six thirty.
Ben: Good. Now we can argue about something real.

title: The Same Rain
paragraphs: Two people can stand in the same rain and have opposite days.
One is a farmer whose field has been dry for a month. The other is a bride whose wedding is outdoors.
Nothing about the rain is different. What differs is the plan it interrupts.
This is why arguments about facts often fail. People are not usually disagreeing about the fact; they are disagreeing about whether the fact is good.
So before asking who is right, it helps to ask what each person needed the day to be.
The rain was the same. The afternoon was not, and both of us were telling the truth.

title: The Tree That Shares
paragraphs: In a forest, trees are connected underground by a network of fungus. The fungus attaches to the roots of many trees at once.
Water and minerals travel through this network. So does sugar, in small amounts, from trees that have more to trees that have less.
Scientists disagree about how much this matters. Some say it is a small effect. Others say it changes how we should think about a forest.
Either way, the old picture of trees as separate individuals is wrong. A forest is a system, not a collection.

title: Why Flowers Have Colours
paragraphs: A flower's colour is advertising. It is not for us; it is for insects and birds.
Red flowers are often visited by birds, because birds see red well. Yellow and blue flowers attract bees.
Some flowers have patterns invisible to humans but visible to insects, because insects see ultraviolet light.
Scent does the same job at night, when colour is useless. That is why white flowers often smell strongest.
So a flower is a message with a target audience. Change the audience, and the message changes.
Colour costs the plant energy, so it only pays when there is a customer.

title: The Ant and the Acacia
paragraphs: In Central America there is a tree called the acacia, and an ant that lives only on that tree.
The tree provides hollow thorns for the ants to live in, and small sweet packets on its leaves for them to eat.
Experiments show that acacias without ants grow more slowly and are eaten more often.
This kind of arrangement is called mutualism. Both sides give something and both sides receive something. Neither could easily live alone.
The acacia also makes a chemical that tastes bad once the ants are gone. The tree is not helpless; it is slow.

title: Should We Bring Back Lost Species?
paragraphs: Scientists can now edit the genes of living animals. Some have suggested using this to bring back extinct species.
The argument for it is that we caused the extinctions, so we should repair them.
A mammoth without a steppe is a zoo animal with an interesting history.
There is also a practical question. Money spent on bringing back one species could protect a hundred that are still here. That trade is the real decision.
And there is a third question that nobody likes. If we bring a species back, where does it live? The place it came from is a road or a farm now.

title: The Plant on My Desk
paragraphs: There is a plant on my desk that I have kept alive for three years, which surprises everybody including me.
It is a small succulent. I water it once every two weeks, and in summer I forget and it survives anyway.
A plant does not need your attention. It needs light and a little water, and then it needs you to leave it alone.
I have killed seven plants learning this. The eighth one is doing very well.
What I learned is that most plants do not die of neglect. They die of kindness. Watered twice a week and moved to a bigger pot, mine drowned in soil that never dried.

title: Why Pandas Are Difficult
paragraphs: Pandas are famous, protected and expensive, and the reason is an unusual diet.
A panda's digestive system is that of a carnivore. It cannot process bamboo efficiently.
So it must eat a lot: ten to fifteen kilos a day, for ten to twelve hours.
This is why pandas cannot travel far, cannot hibernate, and cannot survive in a small reserve. They must always be near a large bamboo supply.
Protecting a panda therefore means protecting a forest, not an animal. This is true of most endangered species, which is why the popular image is misleading.

title: The First Dish I Cooked
paragraphs: The first dish I cooked alone was tomato and egg. I was eleven and my mother was ill.
I had watched her make it a hundred times, so I was confident. I put the oil in, then the egg, and the pan caught fire slightly.
I turned off the gas and put a lid on it, which is what she always did. The fire went out.
The dish was not good. The egg was dry and the tomato was raw. My mother ate all of it.
I can make it properly now. It took about ten attempts and one serious conversation about heat.
The serious conversation was about one thing: the pan must be hot before the egg goes in.

title: Why Recipes Use Exact Amounts
paragraphs: A recipe says two hundred grams of flour and one teaspoon of salt. A grandmother says a bowl and a pinch.
Both work, and the difference is feedback. A grandmother cooks the same dish every week and adjusts by eye.
A recipe is written for someone who cannot adjust, so it removes the decisions.
This is why baking recipes are exact and stir-fry recipes are vague. Baking is chemistry: the ratio decides the result.
A stir-fry can be corrected halfway through. A cake cannot. Exactness appears where correction is impossible.

title: The Soup That Takes Four Hours
paragraphs: My uncle makes a soup that takes four hours. He starts at nine in the morning for a lunch at one.
The first hour is only bones and water, boiling hard, then poured away. He says this is the most important hour.
The next three hours are low heat. The pot barely moves. He adds ginger, then nothing else.
At the end there is salt, added in three small amounts, tasting in between.
I once asked why he does not use a pressure cooker. He said it takes twenty minutes and tastes like twenty minutes. I did not argue.

title: Food and Memory
paragraphs: Food is one of the strongest memory triggers, and the reason is partly chemical.
Smell goes directly to the part of the brain that handles memory and emotion, bypassing the usual relay station.
But there is a social layer too. The dishes we remember are the ones somebody made for us, repeatedly, at a particular time of life.
So a recipe is never only a recipe. It carries the person who cooked it, which is why families argue about the correct way to make things that taste identical.
Two sisters can cook from the same recipe and each will say the other has it wrong.

title: At the School Canteen
paragraphs: Ben: What is that? Amy: Fish with tofu. It is better than it looks.
Ben: It looks like nothing. Amy: Try it. The sauce is the whole point.
Ben: All right. (tastes) That is actually good. What is in it?
Amy: I asked once. The cook said soy sauce, ginger and something he would not tell me.
Ben: So it is a secret. Amy: It is a canteen. It is probably sugar.
Ben: Ask him again. Amy: I did. He said the secret is the order you put things in.
Ben: That is not a secret, that is a sentence. Amy: He knows. He was smiling.

title: Cooking as a Life Skill
paragraphs: Schools teach algebra for six years and cooking for one term, if at all. This is a strange set of priorities.
Cooking is not a hobby. It is the skill you use every day for the rest of your life, and the one that most directly affects your health.
And it teaches failure. A dish that goes wrong is visible, immediate and not serious. That is a good way to learn that mistakes are survivable.
So one term is not enough, and it should not be optional.
Someone who can cook four dishes can feed himself for life. Someone who cannot depends on other people's moods.

title: The Plan That Worked
paragraphs: In September I made a plan to improve my English. It had one line: twenty minutes a day, before dinner.
No app, no list of grammar points, no weekly test. One line and a fixed time.
I missed four days in the first month and eleven in the second. I did not restart the count or punish myself.
By January I had read two short novels in English. Not well, but without stopping.
The plan worked because it was small enough to survive a bad day. Every plan I made before this one failed for the opposite reason.

title: Why Plans Fail
paragraphs: Most plans fail in the second week, and the reason is almost never laziness.
The first cause is size. A plan that needs ninety minutes cannot survive a Monday.
The second is vagueness. Study more is not a plan. Study page forty to forty-five at eight o'clock is.
The third is all-or-nothing thinking. One missed day becomes a failed plan, and a failed plan becomes permission to stop.
So a good plan has three features: it is small, it is specific, and it assumes you will miss days. The last one is the one people forget.

title: Two Lists
paragraphs: There are two kinds of list, and mixing them up causes most of the stress in a school week.
The first is a task list: things to do, in no particular order. It has no times and no end.
The second is a schedule: things to do at particular times. It is fixed and it can be full.
A task list is for choosing. A schedule is for doing. Confusing them means either a list you never start or a day with no room.
The method that works is simple: write the tasks, pick three, then put those three into times. Three, not ten.

title: What I Want in Five Years
paragraphs: Our teacher asked us to write where we want to be in five years. Most of the class wrote a job. I wrote a sentence about a room.
I wrote that I want a small room with a desk by a window, and enough time to read in the evening.
I have kept the sentence. It is more useful than a job title, because it tells me what to check before I accept anything.
A goal is easier to reach if you describe the life around it, not only the work inside it.
So my picture has a small kitchen, one shelf of books, a window facing east, and work that lets me be home by seven.

title: Asking for Advice
paragraphs: Student: I want to improve my maths but I do not know where to start.

Teacher: Then start there. Not at chapter one. Student: But I do not understand chapter one either.
Teacher: You probably do. Chapter one is what question one to eleven asked.
Student: So I should do the questions I got wrong? Teacher: Ten of them, tonight. Not the whole book.
Student: Ten, tonight. Teacher: And the same ten tomorrow. Student: The same ten? Teacher: Until they are boring.

title: The Timetable on the Wall
paragraphs: My cousin has a timetable on her wall. It is not a school timetable. It is hers.
She drew it herself: seven columns for the days, and rows for the hours from seven in the evening to eleven.
Some boxes are filled with subjects. Some say rest, and one says nothing at all, every day, from nine to half past nine.
I asked about the empty box. She said, that is the box that makes the rest of it possible.
I copied the idea. It is the only study method I have ever kept for more than a month.
It hangs above my desk and it is not beautiful. It is honest, which is better.

title: The City in 2050
paragraphs: Predictions about cities usually fall into three groups: transport, energy and food.
Transport is the easiest to predict. Most cars in 2050 will probably be electric, and many will be shared rather than owned.
Energy is harder. Solar and wind will be cheaper, but storing electricity is still the unsolved problem.
Food is the most uncertain. Vertical farming works for vegetables and costs too much for grain.
So the honest forecast is uneven. Some parts of daily life will change completely and others will look almost the same.

title: The Prediction That Was Wrong
paragraphs: In the 1960s, many experts predicted that by the year 2000 nobody would work more than twenty hours a week.
Machines would do the labour. People would have a problem: too much free time.
The forecast was half right. Machines did take over much of the work.
But the working week did not shrink. The saved time went into new tasks that nobody had imagined, and into being available all the time.
The lesson is not that prediction is useless. It is that prediction usually gets the technology right and the human arrangement wrong.

title: Learning to Drive in 2040
paragraphs: My father learned to drive in 1995. He says the hardest part was the clutch.
I will probably learn in 2040, and the car may not have a clutch, or a steering wheel, or a driver.
This is strange to think about. A skill that was once necessary may become a hobby, like riding a horse.
But somebody will still need to know how it works, because machines fail and somebody has to decide what to do.
So I will learn to drive anyway. Not because I will need to, but because I want to understand the thing that moves me.

title: The Job That Does Not Exist Yet
paragraphs: Half the jobs people do today did not exist fifty years ago. This is not an unusual situation; it is the normal one.
New jobs usually appear where two old things meet. A data analyst is a statistician who works with computers.
A user experience designer is a psychologist who works with software. A drone pilot is a photographer who works with aircraft.
So predicting future jobs is less useful than noticing which two fields are beginning to overlap.
The skill that survives is not a specific tool. It is the ability to learn the next tool.

title: Talking About the Future
paragraphs: Amy: Where do you think you will be in ten years?
Ben: I have no idea. Somewhere with a job, I hope.
Amy: That is a very low bar. Ben: It is a realistic one. Ask me a smaller question.
Amy: All right. What will you be doing next summer?
Ben: That I can answer. I will be studying for the entrance exam, and complaining about it.
Amy: Do you think you will stay in this city? Ben: Probably. My parents will not move.
Amy: And if you had to leave? Ben: Then I would leave. It is not a decision I can make now.

title: Why We Like Disaster Films
paragraphs: Disaster films are popular, and the reason is not that people enjoy suffering.
In a disaster film the world becomes simple. There is one problem, it is visible, and everybody agrees what to do about it.
Real problems are not like that. They are slow, disputed, and caused by things we are not willing to change.
So the film offers a relief that real life does not: a clear enemy and a clear ending.
This is also why the films are less popular when real disasters are in the news. Fiction needs distance to be entertaining.

title: The Message I Should Not Have Sent
paragraphs: Last year I sent a message to a friend at eleven at night. It was three sentences and it was angry.
I wrote it in two minutes and read it once. I did not read it aloud, which is the mistake.
In the morning she had replied with one line: I do not understand what you are angry about.
I read my message again. She was right. It was angry about something I had not named.
We talked for an hour that afternoon. Now I have a rule: no message about feelings after ten o'clock.
The rule has saved me twice. Both times I was right, and the message would still have made it worse.

title: Why Text Messages Cause Trouble
paragraphs: Text removes three things that speech depends on: tone, face and timing.
Without tone, a short sentence reads as cold. Without a face, irony looks like seriousness. Without timing, a pause becomes a silence of hours.
This is why people add emojis. They are not decoration; they are a substitute for tone.
So the rule is simple. Anything with feeling in it should be said, not typed. If it must be typed, add the tone in words.
Three lines of text have no face, no pause, and no way to take a word back. A voice can soften a sentence while it is being said. A screen cannot.

title: Listening Is Not Waiting
paragraphs: Most people think they are good listeners. Most people are waiting for their turn to speak.
The difference is visible in what happens next. A person who was waiting replies to their own thought. A person who was listening replies to yours.
It also requires silence. If you answer within one second, you were not listening; you were preparing.
This is a skill you can practise, and the practice is uncomfortable, because it means being quiet while somebody finishes a sentence you have already understood.

title: The Group Project
paragraphs: Our group had four people and one problem: nobody would say what they actually thought.
The first meeting produced a plan that everybody agreed with and nobody believed in. We all knew it was weak.
So I asked a different question. I said, if this fails, what will be the reason?
It took ten seconds for somebody to answer, and then everybody talked at once. The real plan came out of that question.
We changed the design completely and got a good mark. The trick was asking about failure instead of asking for opinions.

title: A Letter of Complaint
paragraphs: Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing about a pair of shoes I bought from your shop on 12 October. The order number is 4471.
After two weeks the sole began to separate from the upper on the left shoe. I have worn them about ten times, in dry weather.
I have attached two photographs. I would like either a replacement or a refund.
I have bought from your shop before and have always been satisfied, which is why I am writing rather than returning them without explanation.
Yours faithfully, Chen Hao
P.S. I have kept the receipt and a photograph of the damaged part.

title: Saying No
paragraphs: Amy: Can you help me with the poster tonight?
Ben: I cannot. I have to finish my part of the report by tomorrow.
Amy: It will only take an hour. Ben: It will take three. Last time it took three.
Amy: All right. Ben: Ask me on Thursday and I will do the whole thing.
Amy: Thursday is too late. Ben: Then ask someone else, and I will do the printing on Friday.
Amy: That works. Ben: Good. I am not saying no to you. I am saying no to tonight.

title: Why Some People Never Ask
paragraphs: In every class there are students who never ask a question, and it is rarely because they understand everything.
The usual reason is the fear of looking foolish in front of thirty people. One bad experience in Grade Five can last for years.
What works is making the question ordinary: asking the class a question nobody can answer, admitting when the teacher does not know, and answering a weak question as carefully as a good one.
The barrier is not confidence. It is the calculation of risk, and the risk has to be lowered by somebody else.

title: The Hour I Do Nothing
paragraphs: Every day at about four, I stop working for an hour. I do not read, I do not watch anything, and I do not sleep.
At first this was uncomfortable. An empty hour feels like a waste, and I kept reaching for my phone.
The strange result is that I get more done afterwards. The hour is not lost; it is borrowed, and it comes back with interest.
My friends think this is a waste of time. I have stopped explaining it. The hour works whether or not anybody agrees.
An hour a day is fifteen days a year. I have never regretted one of them.

title: Why Free Time Is Not Free
paragraphs: Free time is the only kind of time that comes with instructions.
We are told to use it well: learn a language, take up a sport, read the classics. A weekend spent doing nothing now needs an excuse.
The trouble is that rest, by definition, cannot be productive. If it is producing something, it is work with better lighting.
So the useful question is not what to do with your free time. It is whether you can spend an hour without answering that question.
Most people cannot. That is why the first twenty minutes feel wrong, and why the hour is worth keeping.

title: Hobbies That Go Nowhere
paragraphs: My uncle collects bus timetables. Not buses, not tickets. The printed timetables that used to hang at stops.
He has about four hundred, from eleven cities, some of them forty years old.
He does not show them to anybody. They are in a box under his bed, and twice a year he takes them out and looks at them.
I asked him why. He said that a timetable is a promise: this bus will come at this time, whether or not you are there.
There is no money in this hobby and no use. He is the happiest person I know.

title: A Weekend Without a Screen
paragraphs: Last month my family agreed to spend one weekend without phones, tablets or television. It was my sister's idea, and we all said yes too quickly.

By Saturday afternoon we had played three games of cards and repaired a chair that had been broken for a year.
On Sunday we walked to the market and bought things we did not need, because we had time to look.
We have not repeated it. But we talk about it more than any other weekend that year.

title: The Value of Boredom
paragraphs: Boredom has a bad reputation, and it is undeserved.
When nothing is happening, the mind starts to wander. That wandering is where new connections are made, because it is not directed at anything.
This is why good ideas arrive in the shower, on a walk, or in the ten minutes before sleep. The mind needs an empty room.
A screen fills that room instantly. It is not that screens are bad; it is that they are always available, and the empty room never gets built.
So boredom is not a problem to be solved. It is a condition that has to be allowed.

title: Learning to Do Nothing
paragraphs: My grandmother can sit in a chair for an hour and do nothing. Not sleep, not think about anything in particular. Just sit.
I tried it once, in her living room, while she was resting. I lasted six minutes.
She asked what I was doing, and I said I was learning to do nothing. She laughed and said there is nothing to learn.
She is right, in a way. There is no technique. The only requirement is to stop looking for one.
I still cannot do it for an hour. I am up to eleven minutes, which she says is progress.

title: The Knee
paragraphs: I hurt my knee in Grade Seven, playing basketball on a wet court. It swelled up and I could not bend it.
The doctor said it was a strained ligament and told me to rest for three weeks. I rested for eight days.
I went back to training too early. The knee hurt for another two months, and I missed the whole season anyway.
What I learned is that the body keeps its own schedule. You can ignore it, but you cannot negotiate with it.
I now rest for the full period, every time. It is boring and it is faster.

title: Sleep Debt
paragraphs: Sleep debt is the difference between the sleep you need and the sleep you get. It accumulates.
Two hours short every night for a week is fourteen hours of debt. One long Saturday cannot repay it.
The repair is not a single long sleep. It is a return to a regular schedule, with the same bedtime every night.
This is why sleeping until noon on Sunday often makes Monday worse. It moves the body clock later, and Monday arrives an hour too early.
The debt is real and it cannot be paid in one long night. It is paid back half an hour at a time.

title: What Stress Does to the Body
paragraphs: Stress is not only a feeling. It is a set of physical changes, and they are useful in short bursts.
The heart beats faster, breathing quickens, muscles tense, and sugar is released into the blood. The body is preparing to act.
Long-term stress affects sleep, digestion and the immune system. People under it catch more colds and heal more slowly.
So the problem is not stress itself. It is stress that never gets switched off. Exercise, sleep and talking to somebody all help switch it off.
The body has one switch, and it is not in the mind.

title: Why Breakfast Is Not Optional
paragraphs: Skipping breakfast is the most common health mistake among students, and the easiest to fix.
After a night without food, blood sugar is low. The brain depends on glucose, so concentration drops first, then mood.
The objection is usually time. But a proper breakfast takes ten minutes, and ten minutes is the difference between one alarm and three.
So the advice is not to eat more. It is to move the alarm back by ten minutes and spend them at a table.
Ten minutes is enough for an egg, a slice of bread and a glass of milk. Not a meal plan, just a floor to stand on.

title: Walking to School
paragraphs: I started walking to school in October, when the bus route changed and the new one took forty minutes.
Walking takes twenty-five. I leave at the same time and arrive earlier, which nobody believes until they try it.
The first week I was tired by the second lesson. By the fourth week I was not.
What I like most is the walk home. It separates the school day from the evening, and by the time I open the door I have stopped thinking about the test.
I still take the bus when it rains. I am not an athlete, and I have no intention of becoming one.

title: The Argument
paragraphs: Last year I had an argument with my mother about a jacket. It lasted three days.
The jacket was not the point. The point was that she had bought it without asking me, and I was fourteen.
For three days we were polite. That was worse than shouting.
On the fourth day she asked me what I actually wanted, and I realised I did not want the jacket at all. I wanted to be asked.
We agreed on a rule: for anything over two hundred yuan, she asks first. I have not tested the rule. I do not need to.
The rule is not really about money. It is about who decides.

title: Why Teenagers Argue More
paragraphs: The increase in conflict during the teenage years is not a character fault. It has a biological base.
The parts of the brain that handle planning and self-control develop last, finishing in the mid-twenties.
So a teenager has a strong accelerator and a brake that is still being built. That is a description of the machine, not an excuse for the driver.
This is why rules work better than lectures. A rule is external structure, and it can hold while the internal one is under construction.
A rule can be argued with. A lecture can only be endured.

title: The Friend Who Changed
paragraphs: My best friend from primary school changed in Grade Eight. It was gradual and it was obvious.
She started spending time with a different group. She stopped answering messages in the evening.
For a while I took it personally. I replayed conversations looking for the moment it went wrong.
There was no moment. People change shape as they grow, and sometimes two shapes stop fitting.
We still say hello. It is not a tragedy, and it took me a year to be able to say that.
The friend I have now is different too, and so am I. Friendship is not a promise to stay the same.

title: Naming What You Feel
paragraphs: People often cannot say what they feel. They say fine, or nothing, or they get angry instead.
Being able to name an emotion reduces its force. This is well documented: describing a feeling in words lowers the physical stress response.
So a useful habit is to say the precise word, even if only to yourself. The vague feeling is harder to handle than the named one.
This sounds like a small thing. It changes what you do next.
Tell a friend you are angry and he stops guessing. Tell yourself and you stop guessing. Vague feelings are loud and unhelpful; named ones can be handled.

title: The Thing I Was Afraid Of
paragraphs: For two years I was afraid of speaking in front of the class. Not nervous. Afraid.
I avoided it by volunteering for written work, which worked until Grade Eight, when the whole class had to present.
I prepared for three weeks. On the day my hands shook so much that I put the paper on the desk and read from it.
It was not good. My voice was flat and I did not look up. But it ended, and nothing happened.
The second time was easier, and the fifth time was ordinary. Fear does not disappear through argument. It wears out through repetition.

title: The Reef
paragraphs: A coral reef looks like rock, but it is built by animals. Each coral is a small animal with a hard skeleton.
The coral animal lives with algae inside its tissue. The algae make food from sunlight and share it.
This partnership is why reefs grow only in shallow, clear, warm water. The algae need light.
When the water gets too warm, the coral expels the algae and turns white. This is bleaching.
A bleached reef is not dead, but it is starving. If the temperature drops soon, it can recover. If not, it dies.

title: Why the Desert Blooms After Rain
paragraphs: In some deserts, a single rainstorm produces a carpet of flowers within two weeks.
The seeds were already there. Some desert seeds can wait years, staying dormant in dry soil.
They germinate only when they receive enough water, which is a signal that there will be enough to finish growing.
The whole life cycle is compressed: flower, seed, die, within a month.
So the desert is not empty. It is waiting. The bloom is a system that has learned to be patient.
The seeds wait years for one good rain. Some will not open at all. They are waiting for the next one.

title: The Night Sky Away From the City
paragraphs: The first time I saw a truly dark sky, I was twelve and we were in the mountains with no electricity.
I walked outside at eleven and could not find the familiar shapes. There were too many stars.
Somebody pointed out the Milky Way. I had seen photographs of it and assumed they were exaggerated. They are not.
I stood there for half an hour, which is a long time for a twelve-year-old with no phone signal.
Now when I look up in the city I can see about twenty stars. I know what is missing, and that is a strange kind of knowledge.

title: Why We Need Wild Places
paragraphs: Cities are designed for people. That is their purpose, and it is not a fault.
But a place designed entirely for people teaches us that the world is ours. A forest teaches the opposite.
In a forest nothing is arranged for your comfort. The path is uneven, the insects bite, the weather changes without asking.
This is uncomfortable and it is useful. It is the experience of being one species among many, in a place that was not built for you.
So wild places are not only for recreation. They correct a mistaken idea about our own importance.

title: In the Cave
paragraphs: The cave was forty minutes from the road, and the last part was crawling.
Inside, the guide turned off all the lights for one minute. This is a standard thing guides do, and it is always worse than people expect.
Somebody laughed, and the sound went away into the rock and did not come back.
When the lights came on, everyone was quiet for a while. Then we walked out, and the ordinary daylight looked like an enormous gift.
The guide said the cave is still growing. A centimetre every hundred years, which means the shapes above us were there before any city on earth.

title: The Old Tree
paragraphs: There is a tree in our village that is said to be six hundred years old. It is a banyan, and its aerial roots have become new trunks.
You cannot tell any more which trunk is the original. There are about twenty, and they all look the same.
I asked an old man whether the tree was really six hundred years old. He said, the tree is not old, the village is old.
I think he meant that the tree has been here longer than any family, and that is what people are actually worshipping.
Nobody knows how old it is. There is no record, only a habit of walking past it slowly.

title: The Earthquake Warning
paragraphs: Earthquakes cannot be predicted. This is one of the few things seismologists agree on completely.
The reason is that the stress builds invisibly, over decades, in rock that nobody can see.
The fast wave is weak and arrives first. The slow wave is destructive and arrives seconds later.
So a sensor near the epicentre can send a signal faster than the destructive wave travels. Cities get ten to sixty seconds. It is not prediction. It is a race between two waves, and the signal wins.
Ten seconds is enough to open a door. Sixty is enough to stop a train.

title: The Flood
paragraphs: The water came up over two days, which is how most floods happen. There was no single moment.
On the first day it filled the low field behind our house. On the second day it crossed the road.
By the evening the ground floor had fifteen centimetres. We moved everything upstairs, including the refrigerator, which took four people.
The water stayed for three days and left a line of mud on the wall that is still there.
People came to look at the line for months. It was the only accurate record of how high it went.

title: Why Some Places Flood More
paragraphs: Two towns can receive the same rainfall and flood very differently. The difference is usually the ground.
Concrete does not absorb water. A city covered in concrete sends almost all the rain into drains within minutes.
A forest absorbs it. Roots and soil hold water and release it slowly over days.
Wetlands do the same job more efficiently. They act as a sponge, and filling them in removes the sponge.
So flooding is often a design problem. The rain is natural; the speed at which it reaches the river is not.

title: The Typhoon Drill
paragraphs: Teacher: When the alarm sounds, we do three things. Listen.
Student: Line up, walk out, go to the hall?
Student: Why not the bag? Teacher: Because a bag in a corridor is a person falling down.
Student: How long do we have? Teacher: The drill should take two minutes. The real thing gives you less.
Student: And the windows? Teacher: Close them, and move away from them.
Student: What about the ones in the corridor? Teacher: They are already closed. That is another person's job today.
Student: And the windows? Teacher: Closed too. Now walk, do not run.

title: Living With Risk
paragraphs: People who live near volcanoes, rivers and fault lines are not ignorant of the danger. They have usually weighed it.
The land near a volcano is fertile. The land near a river is flat and watered. The land near a fault line is often cheap.
What changes the trade is preparation. A house built to resist shaking, an agreed meeting point, a bag by the door.
The question is never whether a place is safe. It is what has been done about the ways it is not.
A city that has done the work looks boring on the news. Drains, drills, notices, and a school that practises twice a year.

title: After the Storm
paragraphs: The morning after the typhoon, the street was covered in branches and one large metal sign.
By eight o'clock thirty people were outside, most of them not talking. Somebody brought a saw. Somebody else brought bags.
Nobody organised it. The work divided itself: the strong cut, the rest carried, the old watched and told people where to put things.
It took four hours to clear the road. The sign was the last thing, and it took nine people.
By noon the street looked normal. That is the part nobody photographs.

title: The Wrong Gift
paragraphs: When I first visited a friend's home in another country, I brought a clock as a gift.
The room went quiet for a second. My friend's mother thanked me politely and put it on a shelf.
Later my friend explained: in her family, a clock is a bad gift. It suggests you are counting somebody's time.
I was embarrassed for a week. Then I noticed that the clock was still on the shelf, and had been wound.
That is the thing about a mistake in another culture. It is usually forgiven faster than the person who made it forgives themselves.
